That it be an instruction to the Select Standing Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines, if it thinks fit, to divide Bill No. 17, an Act respecting the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, into two Bills.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
With reference to this motion I have the honour to submit the following:
The motion referred to asks the House to give power-by instruction-to the Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines, to divide Bill No. 17 into two Bids.
This Bill was referred to that committee on February the 15th instant, and is con-

sequently in the possession of the committee and is not on the Orders of the House.
On the subject of instruction to committees, May (11th edition, page 48), states that an instruction is necessary to enable a committee to divide a Bill into two Bills; but (see page 481) he further states that:
A motion for an instruction which seeks to confer upon a committee of the Whole House power to make amendments in a Bill that is already possessed by the committee is out of order and this rule applies to instructions to standing' or joint committees.
Bourinot iiiferentially sustains this position on page 651, 3rd edition, where it is * observed that an instruction to a committee should be moved as soon as the Order for the committee has been read by the Clerk, showing that the Bill must then be in possession of the House when instruction is given.
In the case of Bill 17, now that it is in the possession of the committee and not of the House, it is not in order to entertain this motion. This Bill being in the possession of the committee, it would be in order for the committee to report the Bill back to the House with such recommendations as are thought desirable, including that of receiving power to divide the Bill into two Bills. The House could then take such action in the premises as it considers advisable.
A resolution of a similar character to the present appears, however, to have passed the House in 1888, the Bill in question being then in the possession of the committee and no notice of motion having been previously given. There was no ruling given by the Speaker on the propriety of the action taken: indeed, the question was not raised.
I do not think that case constitutes a precedent and consequently I have ruled as above.
Do I understand, Mr. Speaker, that your ruling is that the Railway Committee, which is possessed of the Bill, should send it back to the House for instructions?

Bill No. 39, to amend the Canadian Patriotic Fund Act, 1914.-Hon. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice)-read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Sevigny in the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I might just repeat the formal explanation I gave in introducing this Bill. The provisions of this amendment empower the corporation to assist incapacitated soldiers who may return from the war, and widows, children and dependent relatives of men who may he killed on active service. It also empowers the corporation to give assistance to the wives, children and dependent relatives of residents of Newfoundland who are engaged on active service in the military or naval forces of Canada. As the Act now stands, the powers of the corporation are limited to assisting the wives, children and dependent relatives of men on active service, so that an incapacitated man is not provided for, nor are the widows and children of the men who may he killed. Furthermore, under the present Act the powers of the corporation are limited to assisting the wives, children and dependent relatives of residents of Canada only.
Mr. CARROLL. Will the relatives of men on active service at the front, who are partially dependent upon the wages of these men, get anything from the patriotic fund?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Act says that dependent relatives may be assisted. I do nor think that the Act makes any express provision for those who are partially dependent.

I understand that applications have been made to certain local committees in different parts of the country for relief from this fund and that the best the applicants could do was to give evidence that they were partially dependent on the wages of their sons and they were refused any assistance.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not very familiar with the actual operation of the Act, but perhaps my hon. friend from Montreal, St. Antoine (Mr. Ames), will explain how the work is carried on.
Perhaps it might be well if the hon. member for Montreal, St. Antoine, would take this opportunity of making a statement of what has been done with the patriotic fund up to date.

If the House desires to have a statement of that character, in my capacity as honorary secretary of the fund, I shall be very glad to give it. The House will remember that towards the end of the last session held in August authority for the creation of this fund was given. At the present time probably ninety per cent of the Dominion of Canada is covered either by branches of the patriotic fund or by auxiliary organizations run on the same lines. We	have an office	in Ottawa	whichacts as a clearing house, and all cases that	are referred to	us are sent	on	tothe	proper organization which	is	abranch of our own	organization	or	an
affiliated association. We adopt, generally speaking, a uniform system in dealing with all these cases and we are constantly sending out from the head office memoranda for the guidance of the various branches. I shall be very glad to deal with any question which any hon. gentleman desires to raise. The story in detail would be a very long one but any questions that any hon. gentleman may wish to bring up I shall be most happy to deal with. The hon. member for Cape Breton, South (Mr. Carroll), raised a point a moment ago. In reply to his question I would say that generally speaking, the local committee of each branch is, within certain limits, a law unto itself dealing with applications for relief. We issue suggestions from the head office to them and we tell them how other branches are operating their relief funds. The principles upon which relief is given are these: The first question that is always asked is " Is the family in need, or would the family be in need if there was no patriotic fund?" If it is found that the fa nily are getting along very well there would be no claim upon the fund. But if it is the case that in consequence of the departure of soldiers for the war a family is falling below the scale of decent subsistence then that family would have a claim upon the fund. The next question which would be asked is: Was the family dependent on the soldier? If a wife and children have been wholly dependent upon a man who has gone to the front there would be no question. If it is a widowed mother who is entirely dependent upon the soldier son who has enlisted there would be no question; she would rank both with the Gov-
ernment and with us the same as the wife and children. But we have a certain number of complicated cases of what you might call partial dependency that are dealt with usually by the local branch committee upon suggestions from the head office. In a case of partial dependency where a son has gone to the war, the question usually asked is: How much does the family fall below the scale of decent subsistence in consequence of this boy having gone to the war? If he has turned in $5 a week and his own board was worth $3 the fund would make up the other $2 and put the family in the same position as they would have been in if the boy had not gone to the front. These cases of partial dependency are rather difficult to deal with, and they are usually taken up by the local committees along some such lines as I have indicated.

How much has been collected and expended?
Mr. AMESj As nearly as we can judge at present, in round figures, there is at the disposition of our honorary treasurer about $2,700,000, and there has been expended to date about $800,000, leaving a net cash balance on hand of about $1,900,000. We have resources which we expect will produce about as much more. Consequently, the fund will probably be self-sustaining to the end of the present year, and it is now mainly a question of securing the co-operation of a few communities that have not as yet contributed, on the basis that all take part in the burden before any are asked for the second time to contribute.
What is the proportion received by dependents of soldiers from the Government in the way of separation allowance, or assigned pay, and that received from the patriotic fund?

In order to answer that question adequately it would be necessary to classify the soldiers' families in this way: first, families of British reservists; second, French reservists; third, Belgian reservists; then Canadian Overseas contingents, and, finally, Canadians who are called out for home service whether they volunteer to go or not. Besides these there are men in the naval service. The Government, in the case of overseas service, gives a separation allowance of $20 a month to every wife or widowed mother. We take a family and consider the question with a view to the cost of living in a particular neighbourhood. We

wo-uld consider that in Montreal a woman with three children, one twelve years of age, one eight, and one four, was entitled to $45 a month from all sources in order to maintain a decent scale of living. The Government gives $20 and the patriotic fund would give her $25. When we get to the western provinces we authorized a scale which is about 25 per cent higher because we found by accurate comparison that the cost of living in Saskatchewan and British Columbia-not so much in Alberta-was about twenty or twenty-five per cent higher than in the large cities in the east.
Where do you draw the line?

At Lake Superior. As a general thing, the rule we have with the local committees is this: Our committees are composed of soipe of the best men in each province, and we say to the committee: determine what you consider to be the amount necessary for a typical family to decently live upon in your province; you can do it better than we can; decide this; fix the amount at $50 or $40 or whatever you may decide upon. The Government gives Canadians $20, the Imperial Government gives Reservists about $15, the French Government about $12, and the Belgian Government gives nothing at all. We make up the difference in each of these cases in order that a family may be enabled to maintain a decent scale of living.

As it appears to me the responsibility of caring for the dependents of men who are serving the country in a military way at the present time rests primarily upon the State and private efforts should not be called upon to more than supplement the provision made by the State. Does the State at the present time undertake the major provision for the dependents of soldiers, or has the major provision to be made up by subscriptions of citizens5 I think it is entirely desirable from every point of view that it should be distinctly understood on all hands that the obligation of maintenance of soldiers' dependents is an obligation Of the state, and that private generosity should not be drawn upon except to a supplementary extent and for supplementary purposes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The separation
allowance established in this country was fixed by reference to that of the United Kingdom, but it was made somewhat larger here than in the United Kingdom by reason
of the fact that the conditions here as compared with those in the old country would justify it. In addition to that, the soldiers in some cases assign a portion of their pay. If I remember correctly, an Order in Council was subsequently passed to deal with cases in which pay was not assigned, providing that a certain proportion of the pay should be appropriated for the support of the soldier's dependents in cases of the character to which my hon. friend has referred.
I shall be glad later on to lay a copy of the Order in Council on the table. It was passed purely for the reason that in a proportion of cases, I think not a large proportion, no portion of the pay was being assigned, and therefore the depend nts were left to be taken care of by the separation allowances, supplemented by the Canadian patriotic fund. It was felt that as the great majority of the soldiers did assign a portion of their pay, and as that seemed the proper course to pursue, an order should be made in regard to it, and an order was so made.

Was the order made to
divert a portion of the soldier's pay to his family?	-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It was made so that a portion of the soldier's pay could be appropriated for the support of his family during his absence.

I have no desire to delay the committee, nor have I any desire to press unduly for information that I am quite aware it would be difficult to get; but this is a far-reaching matter, and I think that here and now is as good a place as any to get a fairly good general understanding as to what are to be considered the obligations of the state and the obligations of private citizens. I do not wish to criticise the Government or the gentlemen who are interested in the patriotic fund to any degree, but I take this opportunity of stating that within the range of my knowledge, and according to my judgment, the conditions of life from which our soldiers have enlisted differ materially from the conditions of life from which were enlisted the soldiers of the United Kingdom, to whose case the separation allowance which was used as the basis of calculation in fixing our separation allowance applied. I do not think that the fact that the present separation allowance was considered a proper allowance in the United Kingdom, under the circumstances existing before this war occurred, was a sufficient ground for believing that a certain percentage of advance

upon that allowance was a proper allowance in Canada when and where the extraordinary circumstances surrounding this war were taking place. The proof that the view I express is correct, is, that the British Government has found it necessary to recognize the new conditions surrounding enlistment in the army for the present war, and have seen fit-and no doubt not without the greatest necessity for it-to revise their provisions in regard to separation allowance. We could not tell beforehand- I do not expect even this Government to know everything in advance-but the war has been in progress for six months; we have had the separation allowance in operation, we have had the assignment of men's pay, we have had the patriotic fund raised generously throughout the country and administered I am sure with the very best of intentions, and I have no doubt capably administered, so that to-day we must know a great deal more about this matter of taking care of the dependents of those who are fighting our battles than we did in August last. While I quite readily accept the amendments to the Bill which we are now considering, I still think that there is necessary a very considerable revision of the provisions which have been made for the maintenance of the dependents of soldiers who are now serving their country, or who may be hereafter expected to serve their country. While I am quite aware that this legislation is not legislation providing for separation allowances from the treasury, I think this is a proper time to put on record the views I hold, and hold very strongly, that time having elapsed, and conditions having become known, it is in order that there should be a readjustment of the statutory arrangements for the maintenance of dependents of soldiers in the service of their country, that would render the efforts of the patriotic fund and those who are interested in it a supplementary source and not, as they appear to me at the present time to be, the principal source of support of the dependents of the soldiers who are at the front. I wish to say, as strongly as I can, that the support of these dependents is the duty of the state, and that the interests of the state require that that duty shall be discharged freely and generously, with, of course, good judgment and care. I hope that there will be legislation both in regard to separation allowances and maintenance of dependents, and that it will be based on conditions as they exist in this country, and as they have been found to exist in the operation of our laws in this matter up to 
the present time, rather than upon the legislation and regulations prevailing in the United Kingdom which were based on a totally different condition of affairs.

It appears to me that the
Government has acted very generously in the matter of separation allowances. As I understand the Government is to-day paying 20,000 separation allowances, while the Canadian patriotic fund is carrying between 10,000 and 11,000 families, so that about half of the dependent families of the soldiers are not coming to the patriotic fund at all. That would go to prove that the Government, in making the basic appropriation of $20 applicable everywhere, was covering pretty nearly half of the cases. To overpay that half would be as bad as to underpay the other half. The Government, moreover, has no flexibility. It would have to pay $20 to a soldier's wife just the same, whether she lived in a rich rural community in the East where the cost of living .was low, or in the Yukon or in a mining district in British Columbia where the cost of living was very high. The Government can not discriminate and say that for this area the separation allowance shall be $20, for that area $25, for that $30, and so on. The patriotic fund comes on afterwards and acts with a great deal of flexibility, on the best local advice that can be secured. It takes each family by itself and asks the simple question: Considering that the family gets $20 from the Government, how much more is needed to bring your family up to a decent scale of existence? One wife may have no family, and $10 added to the $20 separation allowance may be all that she requires. Another wife may have ten children, and the patriotic fund takes into consideration the fact that this woman needs a great deal more to support her than the first, although the Government gives both the same separation allowance. The Government has acted very wisely in giving a basic $20 to each dependent family whether it needs it or not, and the patriotic fund follows only in cases where further assistance is required.
You have only to read the casualty lists to see how many of our soldiers have their next of kin in the old country. For those families probably $20 is enough, and we do not send any money to England from the patriotic fund, because it is apparently not necessary to do so. The few cases of hardship that we hear of in England are pro-

vided for by reciprocal arrangement with the Soldiers' and Sailors' Relief Association. We care for the wives and dependents of old country reservists here, and that Association cares for our soldiers' wives and dependents in the old country in cases where $20 is not quite sufficient.
This combination of Government effort and local philanthropy works extremely well. It has been a great blessing to many people in Canada to have an opportunity to contribute to the patriotic fund. It has done many people a world of good, because many a one who could not fight wanted to have an opportunity of helping in some way. Many a man, who is saving from month to month and making a monthly contribution, has the satisfaction of knowing that, while he does not go to the front himself, he is providing for the wife and family of some other fellow who has joined.
Mr. W.H. BENNETT: This discussion will perhaps clear the air a little in the province of Ontario. The Toronto evening papers, which as a rule are very widely
4	p.m. read bf the working classes, have been filled with letters in regard to what is being paid in the way of separation allowances. I regret that a great many of these letters have been anonymous, but I am sure a full statement has not yet been placed before the people of this country as to how the different funds stand.
According to my information, the amounts payable to-day to officers and privates are as follows. A major is paid $150 a month as pay, and receives in addition a separation allowance of $60, making a total of $210 a month. A captain is paid $105 a month, plus a separation allowance of $20 a month. A lieutenant is paid $75 a month with a separation allowance of $40 a month. A private draws about $35 a month, with a separation allowance of $20 a month. If these men hand over all their Wages to their families, it means that the family of a major receives $210 a month, the family of a captain $155 a month, the family of a lieutenant $150, and the family of the man behind the gun $55. In my town, and in many other towns, tho admirers of the man behind the gun consider it unfair that the wife of a major should be drawing $210 a month foT pay and separation allowance, while the family of the poor private gets only a total of $55. I would ask the bon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) wiiat proportion of this fund so far has gone to the families of officers, and what amount
approximately to the families of privates, and also, if the statement is correct-because I have seen it so stated in the newspapers- that in any town where no contribution has been made to the patriotic fund, any person being the relative either of a private or of an officer who makes application to the patriotic fund is told: As your town has not contributed to this patriotic fund, you are stopped from participation in it. If such is the case, it is unfair, in view of the fact that the Government has paid a considerable amount towards this fund.
It has paid nothing.

I understood there was a vote last session, but I am in error as to that. The wife and family of the private should get more money from the separation allowance, because his pay is so small as compared with the pay of an officer.
Was the hon. gentleman right in stating that the Government had paid something towards the patriotic fund?

I was in error as to
that. I thought that it had contributed $1,000,000 last session.

The Government has contributed nothing whatever to the patriotic fund. Many municipalities and towns have been extremely generous, and so have individuals.
I do not think we have on our list a single case of a major or any one of higher rank than a major receiving assistance from the patriotic fund. A case might arise_of some sudden call being made on the wife of a major, in his absence, for an insurance premium or something of that 'Sort. In such a case the patriotic fund might make a special grant. Generally speaking, we have assisted very few officers. Some captains' and lieutenants' families have been assisted; but every case in which an officer's family has been assisted has been made the subject of inquiry by a special committee at Ottawa. It has been said that, if persons write from a community that has given no subscription to the patriotic fund, they are likely to get a reply to the effect that the fund refuses to assist them. That is putting the matter rather baldly, but there is a germ of truth in it. Where a community, like the county of Simcoe, for example, has through its county council set -apart a vote of $25,000 for the patriotic fund, $4,000 of which has been distributed and $21,000 of which is not being distributed as yet in any way, if that community writes asking us to

take eare of some of its cases, we are very liable to reply: " Take care of your own." Wherever it has been impossible to create a local organization-and there are two towns in Canada, so far, that have absolutely refused to do anything for their people-we have selected a leading patriotic citizen in the town and asked him to administer our fund, and we send him each week all that is needed for the soldiers' wives there, even though these towns have never given a dollar and never will.

I forgot, while on my feet, to make a statement regarding my own town. Before this patriotic fund was launched and circulars sent out, an appeal was made-as I recollect it-for the Hospital Ship Fund. In my own town that was resoonded to very liberally-I think nearly $1,000 was subscribed. Then came the Belgian fund, and I think that upwards of $700 was subscribed for that; so the town was not doing badly. When the further appeal was made for the patriotic fund, in view of the fact which was well-known, that the officers and soldiers were going along the line of the figures I have given and they, the soldiers, had, in the main, given their pay to their families, it was thought it would be difficult to launch a third contribution for the patriotic fund. For that reason the town of Midland did not make any grant to the patriotic fund. As to the grant of the County Council of Simcoe, I have not the details of that grant before me, but I understand that' it was apportioned so much to the patriotic fund, so much to the Belgian relief fund and so much for these other funds, all of which have in view the laudable purpose of assisting those engaged and who have suffered in the war.
Mr. MARCIL; Could the hon. member for St. Antoine give us the figures by provinces?

I could not give that exactly up to date. But up to the 1st of February, the cash actually received here amounted to about $1,035,000 for Quebec, $1,010,000 for Ontario, and contributions from the other provinces the amounts of which I do not recollect, making a total of about $2,500,000. Since then we have been in receipt of very large subscriptions from many places in Ontario, and to-day Ontario has probably subscribed $1,250,000 and Quebec about the same.

There is a very laudable
emulation between the two provinces in this matter.
There is.
Could the hon. gentleman also give us the amounts subscribed to the other funds by Quebec and the other provinces?	*

I see in the press at various times statements as to aid being refused from the patriotic fund to wives of men who have gone to the front if the marriage took place after enlistment and after a certain date. I would like to know if there has been any such refusal, and what the position of the fund is in regard to a soldier who has married, no matter what date.

The fund has followed exactly the path blazed by the Government in that respect. The Government gave notice, about the middle of January, that after the 28th of January, it would not recognize marriages which took place after enlistment, except in special cases certified to as having taken place with the consent of the colonel commanding. We recognize the family as the Government recognizes it for separation allowance.

Looking at the statute passed in August last, 1 do not find in section 3 any power to discriminate in the matter :
The object of the fund is to assist in case of need the wives, children and dependent relatives of officers and men who may be in active service.
I very much doubt the wisdom of the patriotic fund declining to assist a woman who may become the wife of a soldier at any time previous to his leaving this country and going abroad. I can see that, from a military standpoint, it may be necessary to make regulations with regard to the marriage of soldiers, as to the consent of the colonel or officers of the regiment. But the idea of the patriotic fund is to assist cases of actual need, and one can readily imagine conditions under which any soldier's wife would oe justified in coming forward for assistance and in expecting that assistance from the patriotic fund.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: So far as the general rule is concerned, my hon. friend doubtless knows that in the British army a certain number of men in each regiment are allowed to marry, and those who marry with the consent of the commanding officer-

Marry "on the
strength of the regiment."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: For those that marry on the strength of the regiment provision is made for the support of their family. But a man who marries without leave is said to marry not on the strength of the regiment, and no provision is made for the support of his wife and family. I know that in garrison towns distressing conditions often arise because women have married soldiers and no provision is made for them under the regulations. I should be glad to lay on the table the Order in Council to which my hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) has alluded. I appreciate the force of what my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) has said, and I hope he will also appreciate the consideration that there has been some apprehension that marriages might be rather hurriedly contracted, especially abroad, and a soldier might occasionally be made a victim in an undesirable way. Some intimation of that was given to the Government, and the Order in Council was passed, I think, by reason of the desire to protect and assist the soldier by some such regulation.

I apprehend that
what my right hon. friend says is that the Order in Council provides for aid being given to the wife where the marriage took place with the consent of the commanding officer.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I cannot remember the exact terms. It was brought to us on the recommendation of the officers of the department, by whom it had been considered very carefully. We also gave it very careful consideration. If I remember it well, it amounted to this, that up to the time the Order in Council was passed all marriages that had been contracted were to be recognized and the families provided for. But after that date there were certain restrictions which we thought reasonable and in the interest of the soldier himself. However, I will bring down the Order in Council, that its exact terms may be brought to the attention of every hon. member of the House.

Will the hon. member for St. Antoine be good enough to explain what course an application for separation allowance has to take? The municipalities of Nova Scotia were asked to forward their contributions to the treasurer of the fund at Halifax, who is the general manager of one of the banks. Applications have been made to the local committee in the town in
which I live. After such an application has been passed upon, is it proper to send it to Halifax, or should it be sent to the central committee of the fund at Ottawa?

So far as Nova Scotia is concerned, we have a provincial organization which has a branch in every one of the eighteen counties. Moneys raised in Nova Scotia are all placed in the bank at Halifax, where they are under the control of the Hon. W. T. White, our treasurer. Halifax once a month makes an estimate of the amount required by the eighteen branches. That is released for distribution, and is sent in bulk sums to the eighteen counties. It is then distributed by the local relief committee, and at the end of the month each local relief committee is expected to give a detailed statement on forms furnished by us. These returns are checked by our accountant and if they are correct then an advance is made for the next month and we again receive a detailed statement.

Have the contributions to
the fund made in Nova Scotia been forwarded to Ottawa?

No, $50,000 is now at Halifax under the control of Mr. White, and it may be either left there or brought here, whichever he wishes to do. We usually leave them a working balance and send each month what they need for any one province. The underlying principle of the patriotic fund is for every community to make a general subscription and to put it all in the common fund. After that every community has a right to draw on the fund so long as there is a dollar there in proportion to their needs. We do not feel that the ability of communities to give in money or in men is always the same. One community may be able to send a large number of men but may not be able to contribute largely to the fund. We do not feel that a community which contributes $5,000 to the fund and draws $10,000 from it is in the slightest degree inferior to a community that gives $10,000 to the fund and draws $5,000.

What arrangement is made as to assistance to wives and families of soldiers when they live in the United States? I think about nine hundred have enlisted from Windsor of whom some two or three hundred come from the United States and their families reside in the United States. They are British subjects and I would like to know if the families of those who reside in the United States are receiving that assistance,' and if so, by what means the assistance is contributed.
