There are funds similar to
ours in Great Britain, in Newfoundland and in the United States and we have a reciprocity of exchange between them. For example, we look after all the wives of British reservists here in Canada and the British Association looks after the wives of Canadian volunteers who have been leifjt in their country. We have a similar arrangement in the United States. The Canadian Society of New York has collected a considerable sum of money in the United States and so likewise has the British Imperial Relief Fund of New England in Boston, where I imderstand our Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) speaks tomorrow night for the benefit of that fund. These organizations take care of all families left in the United States of men who enlist in our Canadian forces and besides that they have, in some cases sent us of their surplus funds as well. So the people referred to in Detroit can be all cared for through the American corresponding agency with which we deal.

Has the separation
allowance been paid to the families of men who did not go with the first contingent? I have heard it repeated on several occasions that a number of men who joined the service when the first contingent was raised, expecting to go to the front, did not pass the final medical examination and were therefore not sent; but in the meantime the names of their wives or families had been handed in for the separation allowance and in a number of cases the separation allowance has been paid. The report I heard was that after the first contingent lelt, for a considerable time, there was no complete list of those who had gone. Matters a'-e being cleared up here in connection with the patriotic fund and I think it well, if that has not taken place, that a statement to that effect should be made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I could not tell my hon. friend at the moment whether any eases of that kind have occurred. Of course if the money was paid under such circumstances it would be through inadvertence and in the belief that the men had gone to the front. I heard some rumour of it myself but was not able to verify it. I shall be very glad to make inquiry and let my hon. friend know later whetner any such instance had actually occurred.

I wish to make a further remark in reply to my hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames). I hold that the respons-
[Mr. Wilcox !
ibility for the maintenance of dependents of soldiers on service is a responsibility of 'the State and should be discharged by the State. My hon. friend says that the Government cannot grade its aid according to conditions and circumstances as can the committee of the patriotic fund. I think my hon. friend is placing a limitation upon the Government which I would not like to place on it. I do not know why a committee of the Government cannot use at least as good judgment with such a fund as this as a committee organized under the terms of this statute. The main point that I want to bring to the attention of the House is that the very fact that these allowances from the patriotic fund are raised or lowered, are given or withheld, according to the judgment of private individuals, puts the fact of the receipt of aid from the patriotic fund on a different basis from an allowance from the State. I do not intend to suggest that it is the intention of the Government to continue to deal with the matter in that way, but if the Government should take such a stand; which is virtually equivalent to saying that the dependents of those who have sacrificed themselves and their prospects for the benefit of the country shall be left as dependents on charity, they are certainly not doing credit to either themselves or the country. The conditions of enlistment for this war are different from the conditions of enlistment under ordinary occasions in military service. We have need to-day of every man who can give his services, whatever rank of life he may be in, We are looking for the best and are not content with anything but the best.

The county council of the county of Essex appropriated $20,000 for this fund. In what way would that constitute charity more than if it had been given by the Government of Canada, to be applied absolutely to the same use?

That is not the point in question. If the County Council of Essex raises $40,000 by taxation, to be applied to the support of soldiers' dependents in that or any other county, it is exactly the same as if the money had been raised by this Government or by a provincial government. But the intent of the patriotic fund is that it shall represent private contributions. I agree with everything my hon. friend has said as to the desirability of there being such a fund, which confers not only a benefit on soldiers' dependents, but affords to

those who are neither soldiers nor dependents the privilege of contributing to the fund for the good of their own souls. But the point is that when that fund comes to be the larger part of the support of the dependents, they are then in the position of being receivers of charity rather than in the position" of receiving payment of a debt which the country owes to them. I want to see the dependents of the soldiers who have gone to the front receive on the responsibility of the state to whom they are giving their services whatever consideration they are entitled to, according to the circumstances of the country and their own circumstances. If over and above that, private individuals or organizations see fit to come forward and supplement what has been done, well and good; it is entirely to their credit to do so. But I still say that the obligation of taking care of dependents of soldiers at the front rests primarily on the state, and that that duty should be discharged by the state as a sacred obligation and, with reasonable limitations, discharged to the full. I have seen it stated in the papers that in some parts of Canada recruiting for our contingents is not as rapid as is desirable. No one need go far to believe that one of the reasons for that is the fact that the dependents of men who have enlisted are not being provided for by the state as an obligation, but are dependent upon the good will and good offices of Mr. Smith or Mr. Jones or Mr. Robertson who holds the position of distributor of the patriotic fund. They do not like that, and we cannot expect them to. We are not enlisting ordinary soldiers for ordinary military service. We are facing a most extraordinary condition, and we must face it accordingly. It is not a time to quibble or to count cents. It is a time when we who ask our fellow citizens to take the risks or make the sacrifices of military service should take upon ourselves the responsibility of saying: The state is behind you, for you are doing the service of the state.

Coming as I do from a riding that has been liberal in its contribution of men for this cause, and not illiberal in its contribution of money towards the patriotic fund, I regret exceedingly that the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) has let it go to the country through this House that those who are receiving advantage from the patriotic fund are the recipients of charity. If it is charity that the dependents of the men at 26
the front are receiving from the Canadian patriotic fund, it follows inevitably that [DOT] it is given not as a bounty, but as a dole to those who are poor and needy. If I catch the meaning of the patriotic fund at al1, it is this: the movers behind the scheme recognized that the state owed to the dependents at home an adequate remuneration in the ordinary conditions of life, but that upon those who were able 'to give and were not able to go there devolved the duty of supplementing this amount in the extraordinary and unusual case. I therefore say that the money that is going to the dependents of our soldiers is not going as a charity. It is going as philanthropy; it may be going as a benevolence; but it is going as the grateful gift of the people of the community, who feel that those who have gone to the front have given much in the cause of the community and of the Empire, and that those who have means and stay at home should contribute to this national fund. In the riding I have the honour to represent, the patriotic fund has never been regarded as a charity. When we made solicitation of the people of Kingston, it was clearly put before them that it was their duty to give, and that we wanted the fund to be the spontaneous gift of a grateful people. And in that city of some twenty thousand people, $50,000, or $2.50 a head, was raised for this fund. As the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) has said, through its elasticity the fund has relieved very much distress. It has a tremendous advantage in that what is being done is not done as the hon. member for Edmonton says, through the good offices of the local organizations, but through a body which acts judicially and in such a way that the needs and requirements of those who receive are not known to the general public. Through the elasticity of the compassionate allowance much has been done to relieve the distress of delicate women and delicate children. Speaking for my own community-if I may be permitted to speak for them, and possibly I should speak for them alone, as my experience in connection with the fund is practi- ' cally confined to Kingston-I may say that the patriotic fund has been a God-send to numbers of people who have been relieved in a most trying time and in such a way that only a few knew their need, and those of us who gave to the fund had the tremendous satisfaction of feeling that we were doing something in the cause of the community and of the Empire.

4M2

I feel that there is a good deal of common sense and sound reasoning in the argument of my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). There is undoubtedly a good deal of dissatisfaction in the country over the distribution of the Canadian patriotic fund. There is a feeling that it is being done by favour, and that those counties which have contributed most generously towards it are securing the best treatment. Some other hon. member has mentioned that help from the fund for the dependents of any man on foreign service, depends entirely on whether his county has sufficiently responded. I might also give a case in point. Some time ago I wrote the secretary of the patriotic fund regarding the case of three English reservists who had enlisted from my riding. They had lived in the county only a short time and were practically unknown there, although they had been in Canada for a considerable period. They left an aged father and mother entirely dependent upon the community. The community did its best for them, and I think has supported them up to the present. I felt that if this fund was to be of any use to the people entitled to be relieved by it, this aged couple had a perfectly good claim against it. I wrote to the secretary of the patriotic fund, and the answer 1 received was that the district of Parry Sound as a whole had not contributed to the fund, and that it was up to me to get busy. The district which I have the honour to represent has contributed, not necessarily to this fund, but to almost every movement along this line and very generously. It has also a fund of its own raised in the district for those members of the regiment who have gone from there, numbering from 150 to 200 men. This fund has been raised locally, and it is kept in case of need for the dependants of those who have gone to the front. It has not, as far as I know, been transferred to the patriotic fund; but be that as it may, the point I raise is that people such as I have instanced, especially English reservists, have gone, leaving families totally without means, and these people ought to receive that money from the patriotic fund, which is due to them regardless entirely of the question whether this or that municipality or district has contributed anything towards this fund.

I want to record my protest against the use of the word "charity." There is absolutely no charity in the patriotic fund from start to finish. When we hear of a branch that is trying to run

it as a charitable organization, we ask them not to do so. Every man throughout this country has two choices-either to fight or to pay. If a man fights, we say to him: "Go, God bless you, and may you return safely." If he does not fight, we say: "Pay; make it possible for some one else to go and fight in your place." The man who goes to the front leaving a wife and child behind him, goes because he has confidence that the people of Canada will care for his wife and child while he is gone. He does not bring home the pay envelope on Saturday night, but it comes all the same, because it is filled with the money that other people are ready and willing to put into that envelope, seeing that that man is fighting the battle for the other man who ought to fight. Every man will not be able to go to the front, but he should be quite satisfied to contribute to the burden of those who do. In the American Civil War it was customary for men to buy other men to take their places in the fighting line. I know a man who bought two other pien to go to the front for him, and paid each man $500 for that purpose. We call for recruits, and when a recruit presents himself, we say: "Do not be anxious about your wife and children; they will be well cared for while you are gone." The Government makes a flat rate allowance, so to speak, for every family and dependent such as I have mentioned. The Government, as a rule, gives the larger part of the amount that the family receive. The average supplementary assistance from the patriotic fund generally runs about $18 per family, taking it for the older parts of the country, and a little more in the northwest provinces. A great many families get only $10 or $15, and some get $20 per month.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: You are speaking of the patriotic fund?

I am speaking of the patriotic fund. What brings up the average is the fact that we have to give larger assistance to the French and Belgium reservists, who get very little from their own Governments. Wherever we can bring any influence to bear upon those in charge of private patriotic funds, we tell them to eliminate everything that may give this work an appearance of charity in dealing with the people. We say: "Tell them that they are getting their 'dividend cheques,' if you like; send the cheques out from the head office; do not make it necessary for the woman ever to come to the head office, except the first time; see that she gets her cheque every month, or oftener because it is just as

much due to her as is the separation allowance cheque which the Government sends." Contented soldiers' wives distributed throughout Canada, living comfortably on what the Government gives and what the patriotic fund adds thereto constitute the best recruiting agencies we can have in Canada to-day. When it becomes necessary to appeal to the people for the third, the fourth and the fifth contingents, the fact that these women have been comfortable all winter and have learned to feel that they can trust the people of Canada to look after them, is going to help to get the remaining men that we so much need.
I want to say one more word and it is for the benefit of my hon) friend from Parry Sound (Mr. Arthurs). It has always been our endeavour to organize committees either in towns or counties, and there are very few counties throughout Canada to-day which have not been thoroughly organized. Parry Sound is one of the few backward counties. The great province of Saskatchewan has 310 branches and so well organized is it that I understand there are but six municipal corporations in the whole province which are not connected with the fund in some way. If they can organize Saskatchewan they can organize Parry Sound. If the people of Parry Sound would create a local organization or would apply to become a branch of the Canadian patriotic fund, even if they only contributed $10 and drew $10,000, we would give them that $10,000 if we felt that $10 was all they could raise, provided we had a medium of distribution that could be recognized and controlled. We could not deal with any organization whose accounts we could not check, because we could not become responsible for them. If Parry Sound will become a branch of the Canadian patriotic fund, the matter of how much money they may send in is of minor importance. Let them send us what they can. The moment they become a branch of the Canadian patriotic fund, we will try to see that they get all the money they, need, but until they do so, and while they take the position that they are going to look after their own people, I do not think we can interfere. The office here does not send out cheques to individual families. It is a clearing house, an organizing force that deals with the branches, and through these branches with the local situation. It stands behind them all, makes up the deficiency whatever it may be, and it is glad and willing to make up that deficiency and to endeavour to carry the gospel of giving into 26i
places that have not yet been covered. We are the central organizing clearing 'house here at Ottawa. We do not pay families, we do not determine how much families should get, we do not send out cheques to Smith, Brown and Robinson in Parry Sound, but we expect the people of Parry Sound to form a local organization there, and if they want $100 or $500 or $5,000 .to care for cases in that county, they will get it.

We have heard enough to date to substantiate the view I hold that this is a question that is not only of national but of Imperial significance; and yet my hon. friend stands up in his place and dictates as to the terms and conditions upon which dependents of men who are serving the country and the Empire shall receive assistance from this legislatively authorized fund. We have a Government in Canada whose business it is to look after these things, to stand in the place of the people of Canada in dealing with the interests of Canada, and it certainly grates on my ear to hear any private individual, ' or any member of Parliament, even the hon. member for St. Antoine, say whether or not dependents of people who have gladly given their services to the country shall or shall not receive aid from this fund. We have been told that in Parry Sound they must look after their own people because they have not formed some organization. In Midland they must do the same because they have not made some subscription. This is not a question of whether they have formed some organization or given a subscription; it is a question of whether the men are serving the country and the Empire. But that is not the question with my hon. friend. It is whether they have gone through some sort of procedure that will be satisfactory to him, and if they satisfy him as to that they may come under the rule.

If a case should be reported in an outlying district of Parry Sound away from Ottawa, how could you tell whether that case was genuine and entitled to receive consideration unless we got assistance from the local authorities?

My hon. friend can answer his own question. My point is that a man who is rendering _ service to the State is entitled to the consideration and compensation of the State for that service and that neither he nor his dependents should be dependent upon my hon. friend or upon any other private individual.

Perhaps the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) is scarcely just to the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames). I think he overlooks the fact that the patriotic fund ivas established by an Act in the War session and that practically speaking the patriotic fund and the work done under the patriotic fund, being an Act of this Parliament, is an Act of the State. I venture to say that to my hon. friend in all good nature. I have a feeling that the House is indebted to my hon. friend from St. Antoine for his explanation of what has been done, and I think the country is indebted to him for what we know to be the very painstaking effort he is bringing to hear upon making the patriotic fund a success, in so far as he can do it in his position as secretary, which I presume has been given to him under the Act of Parliament passed at the War session. I say this in a spirit of fairness and as expressing what I really feel is due to my hon. friend in this matter. Unfortunately, imperfection is a mark of humanity, and it would be difficult to invent any machinery which would work with absolute precision. So far from detecting anything dictatorial in what my hon. friend has said, I feel personally indebted to him, ' and I am very pleased to express my opinion.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
- THE BUDGET.
Consideration of the proposed motion of Hon. W. T. White, (Minister of Finance) for Committee of Ways and Means, resumed from February 23..

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to follow the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) in this debate. Before beginning my remarks in reply to him, I should like to pay the Minister of Finance the best compliment I can, in view of his magnificent handling of his great historic Budget in a masterly, comprehensive,' and entirely satisfactory manner. It is true, it is possible to find fault; it is indeed only too easy to find fault anywhere. I have been rather surprised therefore by the remarks, although I enjoyed the speech as a whole, of the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), because he has expressed the policy largely of dissatisfaction at large, and in crystallizing his views he has laid down what may be called two main principles of dissatisfaction, to one of which I shall pro-
[Mr, Oliver |
ceed to refer. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) said:
But it is surely elementary, if our revenues are declining and if there is no other prospect than that they will continue to decline for an indefinite period, that it is the part of wisdom
to introduce measures of economy of a substantial nature.
That meaijs, if it means anything, that instead of spending money during this trying time to enable the people of this country to earn their daily bread on public works, when they cannot earn it on private works, he would prefer to see them tramping the streets in unemployment. I know perfectly well that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) does not mean that, but that is what he has said, and it shows how dangerous it is-if I may be permitted to judge so eminent a man as the hon. member for Edmonton-simply to oppose because you are in opposition. It would be far better for him, and better also for the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) to have taken the Minister of Finance and the rest of the Government party into their confidence, and told them how to construct this Budget, and wherein they are in error, and then supply details of reconstruction. They have done nothing of the sort; they have simply found fault. As I have said, it is easy to find fault-look at the weather; if they want scope for their feelings, let them turn their invective on the weather. Look also, if you will, at the universe-we find a lot of serious things happening, such as the earthquakes in Italy, for which we are in no way responsible. If these gentlemen want simply to find fault why not find fault there. It is very possible to find fault in such case, because it would seem according to the natural forces which work themselves out under Divine guidance, but these are things that pass our understanding, and if we cannot do better the least we should do is to keep quiet.
I would like also to pay a little attention to the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean). He made a tremendous deliverance in its way, but it was fired almost altogether in the wrong direction; but he was not firing at the enemy, he was shooting up in the air. The question was asked by Mr. Wilcox:
Does my hon. friend think there ought to be a duty on tea?
Mr. Maclean: I do not think there ought to be any special duty or stamp tax on anything.
Immediately afterwards Mr. Maclean goes on to say:
Now, what should* be the main features of a war revenue tax? It should be made as much

as possible on articles relatively cheap and of universal consumption.
Do I understand that tea is not of universal consumption? Perhaps the hon. gentleman refers to water. In any event, he has not made himself clear, nor has he taken us into his confidence and provided us with the details of a better Budget. Mr. Middlebro asked, very pertinently, I thought:
Will the hon. gentleman give us his method of raising the taxation, which will measure up to the test which he has just suggested?
Mr. Gauvreau sprang into the breach and said:
It is your duty to give it to us.
That is his idea of fulfilling his duty as a member of Parliament. If you cannot make any capital for your party, try to throw the other side into confusion; but do not remember that you were sent here by a grateful country to do the best you can for it. Raise a row; make a disturbance; split the whole affair up, and then when asked for an opinion say: Oh, you go on and give it; I do not know anything about it at all. That is the purpose which the hon. member served in making that statement. Mr. Maclean, however, said:
My contention is that there is no necessity for any tariff increases. Surely the hon. gentleman must admit that, if the Government which he supports had administered properly the financial affairs of this country, we would not have had a $60,000,000 deficit this year, and there would not have been an estimated deficit of $80,000,000 for next year.
Mr. Middlebro:	The same would apply to
every country in Europe.
Mr. Maclean: Some time, when I have nothing else to do, and the hon. gentleman wants to know how I would arrange a tariff that would yield additional revenue under the circumstances prevailing to-day, I might do so, but I am not inclined to do so at the present moment.
Nor did he at any other time. Surely that is a fair question. We are living under conditions which the hon. member helped to create; and yet when he is fairly asked how he would construct a Budget or a war tariff under these circumstances, at the very moment of his criticism he absolutely declines to give us any consolation whatever, and takes his seat amidst the general confusion which he-has created.
To my mind the most important reference in the Budget was to unemployment. Wars may come and wars may go, but the great war against unemployment continues with us at all times; it is perennial. I am not referring, of course, to shiftlessness or incapacity, to insanity or any other weakness of that nature. I am referring to economic unemployment; and I maintain that it is the great break-down of modern civilization, to which it is our duty, as indicated by the Minister of Finance in his Budget, to turn our im meal ate attention and to let it be no longer a reproach to our twentieth century civilization.
In the thirteenth century the people were in the midst of no such economic difficulties. Every man was his own manufacturer, his own farmer and his own consumer. He lived upon the land; he worked it; he was beholden to no man. He contributed, even though he were a serf, a slave, to the general fund of the little settlement or to the lord of the manor, but he had his indefeasible rights. He paid no rent and he owed no tax further than that to any man. There was never any unemployment.
5	p.m. When he wanted wood, he went out and gathered it. When he wanted food, he went out and raised it. If he, by good fortune, had cattle, he had plenty of meat, milk and cheese. During his spare hours he did a little work perhaps as a smith. He was occasionally a carpenter or a stonemason or something of that sort. Every one was free to do as he liked. The consequence was that, except for those people who were perhaps shiftless-and they were very few-there was no economic unemployment. But later on there arose a different condition. People became divorced from the land by reason largely of the great plague of 1347, when nearly half of the people of Great Britain died. The consequence was that labourers were few. The harvest was naturally still great and the labourers chose to assess the value of their services at a higher rate, and the famous statute of labourers preventing them from doing any such thing was brought in by an alleged parliament of landlords and monopolists. This scattered the labouring class throughout the country in confusion. They were no longer upon the land or off the land. They had no standing, and to this day the great class of labourers has no particular standing in the country except what it is forcing from time to time upon the Government. There was no recognition of an economic standing. Why is it that there has been so much trouble? Why is it that in the midst of plenty, in the midst of a great and rich country where there ought to be such profusion, there is so much need? The taking of profit and the desire to take profit are, in my opinion, the sole

cause of economic unemployment. What is profit? Profit is the taking of that for which we give no true equivalent. If we gave a true equivalent there would be no profit. Take the case of ' making money.' A man makes money when he takes out money that he has not put in. If he takes out only what he puts in, counting his own labour, he will be extremely dissatisfied. The mote he takes out the better pleased he is. If by putting in $5,000, a man can take out $50,000, he is considered a genius; whereas what he has done is he has robbed some one else of that money, because it is a mathematical impossibility that he can put in $5,000 and take out $50,000 without taking the difference from some one else. The alleged stimulus to modern industry has been the taking of profit. This is what the whole system of modern industry has been built upon; and the consequence of its being so large a factor in modern industry and a direct cause of economic unemployment, is that the whole modern system in regard to labour and economic unemployment is mere anarchy-and so it is.
What is the source of value? There is but one source of value-labour cost. Sometimes it is hinted that there is another- monopoly. But, of course, monopoly is not an economic source of value. If the people choose to allow monopolists to take possession of that which they did not earn, if they choose to allow these monopolists to place themselves in the position of lording it over the whole community and so exact tribute, they may. But it is unscientific, it is uneconomic, it is not sensible. Monopoly is in no sense a cause of value. Labour-cost and labour-cost alone, is the cause of value.	Labour produces"
all wealth.	Wealth includes capital,
which, of course, is wealth in the form of money and money only. Labour, the working world, as we know, can produce in two days a week of eight hours each, enough and to spare for everybody in the world. These calculations have been made by statisticians; they are no guesswork and no dream. But the people who desire to take profit know that if they are to have profit they must create profit, and to create profit it is necessary to make things dear; and they proceed to do this in the only way in which it can be done- by limiting the supply. And by limiting supply you cause economic unemployment. Is not that clear? I think it is. So, we have the taking of profits linked up with economic unemployment and shown to be its sole cause. There should be no 
anxiety in the minds of the human race for food or raiment. There is enough and to spare; there is profusion, even luxury. But we are like a man stooping down to drink at a little stream flowing from a great lake. He thinks there is plenty and to spare; but some one comes along and says: I will take possession of the lake and charge you so much a cup for the water. The moment it is sought, by monopoly, and by means of taking profit, to make others pay, the troubles begin and one man becomes practically the slave of the other.
You see, the disposition always is for profit to limit supply. If it he urged that sometimes mills shut down in order to avoid loss and not to limit supply, it may well be replied that this is true under present conditions. But if we were to begin production all over again, no capital would be employed except where it is needed, none would be employed where it would be imperilled in any way, but it would be used entirely for the purpose of production. So, shutting down to avoid loss, like shutting down to make a profit, would be eliminated.
That part of price which is unearned means a profit that is wrongly taken. I admit that it is taken; I admit that there is practically no hope of anybody giving it up. But I do say, and I say it here because this is the proper place to say it, with reference to unemployment, there is no use of discussing free trade, protection or any
o.ther abstract question unless you come to the fundamental principle and see to it that people give a fair equivalent for what they get.
The theory of Ricardo, the founder of modern political economy, was altogether an assumption that political economy depended upon the theory of rent. Adam Smith, in his Wealth of Nations, argued that the wealth of nations would depend altogether upon freedom of trade and upon its twin monster, freedom of labour competition, which is absolutely essential to free trade and which must accompany it as its shadow must accompany any substance. Free labour competition is the basis, the source, the vital cause of distress. It has followed necessarily in the wake of free trade; and if free trade were deliberately, truly and correctly carried out, it would absolutely put the world in the power of money and make slaves of the labour market.
Thorold Rogers and men of that description gathered a priceless treasure of records from the vestries and other storehouses of records of life in England, records of the accounts and work of the people of England

for six centuries. And it was upon such records that Herbert Spencer was enabled to base his tremendous generalizations. Herbert Spencer, however, makes human progress depend upon natural evolution, which is a reversal; it takes it out of our hands altogether except as a normal outcome of our everyday proceedings. Karl Marx, the author of Capital-and I would commend the reading of that work to anybody who has not read it; it will take him three months night and day to read it; it is almost like a work on algebra; but it is worth all the trouble; Karl Marx has analysed, dissected and described every known economic phrase. But, strange to say, he has left them at that. Then, we have the French school-Fourier, Saint Simon and others-who insisted that the remedy for all this trouble is in the socialistic state and who declared that until we have the socialistic state as the owner of the machinery of production, exchange and transportation, there is no way out of the difficulty in which we find ourselves. Then come the Germans. The Germans believe in matter and force-gross modern materialism. They are the apostles of the strictly modern propaganda. Believing in matter and force, they have given an exhibition of it at the present time such as ought to satisfy anybody who likes that sort of thing.
Modern unemployment dates from the time when England invented, monopolized, and patented practically all the modern means of economic invention. Great Britain had a monopoly of this sort of thing. The consequence was that slje wanted the rest of the world to give her the means of gratifying her desire to extend her trade in these particular goods. The rest of the world was then just awakening to the necessity of modern industrialism, but had no means of gratifying it. Great Britain had the whip hand with her system of patent rights, with her knowledge of the inventions which .she herself had made. It was this monopoly that gave her that place of pre-eminence which she has so long enjoyed. She had the Corn laws. In 1846 it was decided to give up the Corn laws, and very rightly so, because the Corn laws were making labour in England expensive, and yet the landlords were getting all the benefit, while doing no good to themselves or to anybody else. So when the Corn laws were done away with food poured in from outside, food became cheap. The agricultural industry necessarily went down and out, but food became cheap, and great industrial organizations were soon in a position, as I say, to
dominate the world. Then began that era of industrial slavery when men and women worked up to seventeen hours a day, and it has taken all the time from that early date to the present to get the day's labour down to nine and ten hours. This shows what a tremendous struggle there has to be in the world on behalf of life and labour against machinery and the desire to make profit. It is a very singular thing, but it shows a philosophic antagonism on the part of many people, it shows a callousness thalt is to be greatly deplored. It will work itself out, it is working itself out in the United States by means of a financial revolution; it worked itself out in France by means of a revolution that tore the country to pieces. These things were foretold, but nobody paid any attention. Why? Because they would rather take profit than listen to the truth. No doubt they will continue so to do, but,' as I have said in reply to the hon. member for Edmonton, it is useless to lament the fact that the incidence of taxation under free trade or under protection goes here, there and everywhere, frequently not to the place's which it should go. It is useless to lament that fact because what I have referred To are the underlying causes of the whole trouble. Manufacturing and money replaced the agricultural landlord and became the new landlord of the modern era. Labour looked back to the land, and the only solution that is proposed of the whole situation at the present time is: " Back to the land! Back to where we were in the thirteenth century." It is made a joke of, people laugh about it because they are insincere about it and frequently do not understand it, but it is a far atavistic cry to something six centuries back, which tells the people instinctively what is the matter; put them back on the land and they will be free, they will be liberated once more.
You take the grandest of all professions, the medical profession, that has conferred more great benefits on mankind by far than all others put together; would there not be a mighty howl of lament and anger if the medical men patented their remedies? Medical men are supposed to make these great sacrifices, to make these great discoveries and inventions which require the profoundest knowledge of science and of the fundamental laws of chemical motion and construction, even the sacrifice of life, yet no one expects the medical profession to patent their rights, because if they did place themselves in the position of the patentee of mechanical rights, the world's last hope would be gone. Surely, if that be
40S

so with regard to the medical profession, it should be none the less so with regard to the feeding and clothing of mankind. If it be so with regard to the curing of mankind, it should be none the less so with regard to the feeding of mankind. Therefore, I say there should be no method of exacting tribute on the cost of food production or the production of clothes that goes on from day to day; it should be absolutely clear of that. People think that unless they are making profit there is nothing in the world, that nobody will do anything. Well, if that is the impelling spirit of any man, all I can say is, God help the man. If he has no more patience, no more unselfishness and no more nobility of character than to throw up his hands when he cannot make profit out of any transaction, then he is fit for Golgotha or some other place of that description, for certainly he is not fit for heaven. Protection is merely control. No one supposes for one moment that protection, which is restriction, is valuable in any other particular, except as a means of control. What is the history of free trade and protection? It is simply this: In the early days, twenty odd centuries ago, when the merchants of Tyre and Sidon, of ancient Greece, of Sicily and Alexandria and Bagdad and Damascus and the East, went about . over the then known world with their Tyrian purple or their finished products, whatever they might be, there was no necessity of discussing free trade or protection, because the people in the countries from which they came fed and clothed themselves. These men were but adventurers, excursionists who went out on .what might be called a side issue. Later on came modern inventions, came the means of making food in profusion, of making clothes in profusion, of wholesale transportation. The danger immediately arose, not that there would be a partial making of goods in one country for another, but that whole mountains of food would be transferred from one country to another, as, for example, from America to France, whole mountains of wools, whole mountains of everything of consequence, so that France would be put out of business by cheapness. The French could go to America and live and buy their food there; but French life and French civilization would disappear; the French people realized this and would not have it, and went back to protection. After 1846 it was felt that the influence of England upon France would result in France adopting free trade. France did so, but she found out, just as I have said, that the result was that her people were being stripped. Take 
China silk. The people of Cevennes used to make silk; they had the silk worms, the mulberry and everything else, and had established a great and prosperous industry. China silk began to come in under free trade, and the people had to stop making silk and fled to the towns. That is what happeed in France; and of necessity they had to stop it by protection, and they put on protection. To-day we must give our people employment. We must keep them at home and make Canada a well-balanced country; otherwise she will be ruined. You say Canadians could get things more cheaply where things are made by cheaper labour or grown more cheaply? So can anybody. But if we are to depend upon cheap labour and cheap production rather than upon the balance of life and production within the country in which we live, we shall become an effete instead of a progressive civilization, and shall soon disappear. From that it follows that this new theory of profit-sharing also is impossible. It might do for a while, but under it men put more money into their pockets than they earn, as I have pointed out. But the idea will remain I suppose, until the people are inspired with some new idea. It is not as in the old Athenian days. Did Socrates teach for gain, did Plato, did Aristotle, did even the Sophists? Not one. It is true that when the jeunesse doree wished to take advantage of their generosity it was necessary for them to adopt means of protection, and they did make a charge.
We have then, if I am right, an exchange of work for goods, for wealth, for food and clothing. Now let us see how this works out. Everything will remain as it is to-day except what? The hours. If you have two days a week with short hours you still have everybody working in the same grade, in the same class, under the same conditions as to-day. Money is still utilized in the same way, and there is no change in exchange or creation or production. There is simply a limiting of the hours of labour in order that all may work. Then all will be able to get work, and there will be still plenty of time left. This is not a Utopian scheme; it is entirely mathematical; you can work it out with a pencil and paper. It is based on economic science, and can be proved or disproved in five minutes, and I therefore ask the Finance Minister's attention to it in the further consideration of his Budget.
I will now touch upon the most extraordinary measure that was ever placed before any country: the British preference.

The British preference is a trade advantage which Canada gives to Great Britain in the Canadian market by means of the the operation of a protective tariff, and without that tariff it could not exist. That means that the Opposition in advocating a preference, British' or any other, are guilty of the wildest stretch of heresy that they could possibly indulge in, because Britain could not get a preference in our market for one minute without a protective tariff. The British prefeienee or any other sort of preference has all the evils of protection, but none of its good points. Why? Because it sends the work out of this country; it sends money out of this country when we import goods; and it leaves the tax-paying to us. That is all. It is a confession that a preference can be given to people by means of a protective tariff, and that is the whole end and aim of protection, which in Conservative hands aims to give that preference to the people at home in Canada. The adoption of the principle of protection is a confession-notwithstanding any arguments to the contrary-that by means of protection you can confer a favour upon a friend; and they propose to confer it upon the British friend. We propose to confer it upon the Canadian friend. That is the only difference. What is the British preference? It is the most un, British thing that ever was concocted-the most absolutely un-British.
There is not a man in England who is not ashamed of the British preference. If is absolutely contrary to the principles of free trade, because absolute freedom of exchange without any preference is the basis of modern British economics. If that is so, you are injuring instead of helping the cause of free trade by giving a preference. You are saying to the British people that in order to establish trade relations with them it is necessary that they should have 'some little by-way or alley, and this you christen the British preference. I do not think there is any excuse for such a thing as a preference. I would sooner see honest square free trade, for a British preference is absolutely unBritish; it is certainly un-Canadian; it is inconsistent and unreasonable. Great Britain gives Canada no preference. Why? Because it is absurd. It is against her idea of economic freedom. She would say that it would be injurious to Canada. And yet for some strange reason we plume ourselves on giving this mighty country of England a preference. We send our work and our money away, and retain the privilege of paying the taxes. If a member of the Liberal party had said that they had to
adopt the preference and not free trade because protection had placed them in an awkward box, they would have had some excuse. But for years they had nothing but a long record of surpluses, and the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) particularly refers to this. He has now turned the tables on us. He says, why do you have these great surpluses taking money out of the pockets of the people? I ask the hon. member for St. John why when he had such big surpluses, he did not adopt free trade instead of giving a British preference? But these gentlemen dared not adopt free trade. The British preference is a two-faced affiair. It is a pretended exhibition of loyalty, and it is a sop to free-traders. It is an apology for having adopted a system of protection instead of free trade. I say that in all kindness and not abusively, but it is nevertheless true and cannot be contradicted. We cannot hope to keep our people employed if on any pretence we send our work out of the country.
The next point I wish to take up is even more practical in its application. I refer to the Eastern peril. Missionaries returning from India and China say that the awakening of those countries to industrial life has been marvelous. China which for 6,000, or at least 3,000 years, has been embedded in a matrix of granite, has changed her whole system of government in practically a day, and she is now a modern republic and ready for the most advanced ideas. Capital (is now pouring in there. They lacked capital, and capital is now pouring in. It is now taking advantage of cheap oriental labour. The capitalist now is asking us to lower the tariff. He asks the Americans to lower their tariff so that he can go to China, erect enormous steel mills and other works and produce cheap goods for the markets of the United States and Canada. Do you imagine that we would be silly enough to allow him to do that? Eight hundred million people are now awaiting to be exploited. They were agriculturists, they dug away with a wooden stick or something of that kind for many years and earned a precarious livelihood. They have learned by means of the missionaries and in other ways the advantage it would be to them to take their place in the van of progress. Railways have disseminated information and established means of interchange and communication. The consequence is that with all these facilities and great natural resources the centre of gravity of modern industrial civilization will be in the Orient as sure as can be unless we keep it in

the West. That is something we cannot impress too strongly upon our people. In this connection I wish to read an article from that intellectual journal, The Globe, which has always seemed to me to be the brains of the Liberal party, with a few exceptions, of course. It says, in an editorial in its issue of January 22:
Terror of good things is one of the peculiar results of distorted economic. A Consul has * warned ' the American Republic that an underwear mill in Hong Kong sells one-half ts entire product in New Work city, that steel rails are being produced in a Chinese modern steel mill with labour that commands only thirty cents a day for ten and a half hours, that Shantung province, with a population of more than 30,000,000, is building modern railways, that in the city of Tsingchau Chinese capital is building a modern steel mill with $10,000,000 invested, and employing labour at twenty cents a day. Instead of rejoicing at the resultant prospect of getting underwear, steel rails, and other products with much less effort than formerly, the reporting Consul regards these things as portentous and even terrible.
This capacity of China to shower blessings or the world is regarded with terror because the reporting Consul has forgotten that the object of industry and commerce is to get underclothing, steel rails, and other products. He thinks the object is to throw obstacles in the way of getting these things and to make it more difficult to supply ordinary wants. The heathen Chinese may be peculiar, but he will not send one single suit or half-suit of underclothing from his gigantic factory or so much as a single knife-blade from his vast rolling mills to the United States unless the people of that republic make something more satisfactory to give him in payment.
Pray, what will they make?
He will do no Zeppelin act to ruin American industry. He will distrbute only as American industry continues able to reciprocate. The more freely he is able to distribute and the more he gives in return for what he receives the more he will lessen the difficulties that make it so hard to produce a living by work in the Republic. The Consul's theory that it is a good thing to make good things hard to get has received a rude jolt by the present belligerent obstruction of trade.
The Globe of January 27 gives further consideration to this question. It says:
The primary purpose of all economic effort, all industry, and all commerce is to obtain things to use and enjoy, not to create difficulties which prevent the accomplishing of that purpose. We must pay for goods from China with our own goods.
What would the Americans pay with, I
ask again? .
The Chinamen's object in manufacturing is not to give, but to get. They want to get our goods. This shows how delusive is the notion that imports or purchases deprive us of work.
It is only as we work that we can purchase.
That is true, and if the Chinese do the work, how are we going to purchase?

The delusion about money leaving the country comes in here, but that is another story. Lvery industral expansion in China or elsewhere is a blessing to the world at large, and especially to the industrial workers. When this is understood and acted upon we will no longer have the paradox of want through an excess of producing capacity and efficiency.
There is the whole question of f^ee trade and the problem of Oriental competition. I thought it wise to submit this to a labour body and I picked out the Peterborough labour body for the reason that the president is the president of the Liberal Association of West Peterborough, the secretary is a Liberal and several members of the executive are also Liberals. It is a large and influential body, it keeps in touch with Toronto, fairly represents the district, and is a very intelligent body as you will presently see. I submitted my course in the House of Commons on the Oriental question to them because, although some hon. members may not remember, I have spoken upon this subject on several occasions. I asked them what they thought of this whole question, and here is what they say:
Peterborough, Peb. 5, 1915. Mr. J. H. Burnham,
M.P. for West Peterborough.
Dear sir,-We, the undersigned, a committee appointed by the Trades and Labour Council of Peterborough to express to you on their behalf the stand taken by them on receipt of your letters of the 22nd and 27th January, do hereby convey to you their wholehearted support of the proposals regarding Oriental labour you are seeking to place before the House.
With the resources of the country developed by intelligent and representative administrations, there is no need for any working man in Canada to be cheap-we have no sympathy with ' Celestial ' ideals of labour.
Tours sincerely,
G. A. Hamon,
Thos. Palmer,
Hugh Robertson,
J. Arthur Sharp.
This, I think, is fairly clear and reasonable. Some little time ago when the British preference first came in, the potters of St. Johns, Que., suffered a serious reverse because they were placed at the mercy of the competition of the potters in the south of Scotland and the north of England. It was from these places in England and Scotland that most of the potters had come to St. Johns, Que. They would go back to the old country but for two things: one is that they have not money enough to go back; the other is that if they did get back they say the prospects are gloomy and they do not want to live as the potters live in Great Britain. I said to these men: " What were you in England-Tories or Liberals?" They said: " Most of us were Liberals." Not hav-

ing an a priori theory, and not being like the man in the fable of ancient Greece who, if he did not fit the bed, had to be made to fit it, they betook themselves to their common sense. They said to us: " If you will raise the protective tariff on sanitary ware in St. Johns, you will give us relief and enable us to go on with our work and live our life and have our being in this country. Here is where we want to live; we like the country, we like the people, we like the climate and we like the prospects. According to his promise not to discuss the tariff, the Minister of Finance could last year give no consideration. He is not at all presenting, as I understood him to say, the war tariff as a protective measure, although it might have that effect. And when the war tariff came forward what do they say? George Smith, as the spokesman of the sanitary ware men in St. Johns, said:
The 5 per cent we have gained should make a difference although the manufacturers are trying to belittle it. I can assure you the operatives recognize that it will help materially, and I myself think it will do so; also the 7 t per cent against the States, even if there "is not so much from these of our own class of works.
There is a concrete case. Here are men not brought up with any protectionist ideas, men brought up with free trade ideas, men confessing that formerly they had been greatly prejudiced in favour of free trade and who now say they do not want free trade; they want to stay in Canada and they want to stay here under a protective tariff, because clearly a protective tariff is good if evenly balanced-I do not for one moment say that a protective tariff which makes a country tight for the manufacturer and the farmer and leaves it wide open for labour is a beneficial protective tariff all around by any means; it is a humbug. You cannot leave it tight for certain things and open for other things and call it an even distribution; that is not an honest distribution. To invite labour from the old country or from anywhere else in here and yet keep the people locked in protection is an iniquity which no one will for a moment stand for. That would not be protection; it would be robbery.
I wish to consider for a moment another very threatening thing known as the menace. I would not have referred to it were it not for the fact that a good deal has been said about it, and I trust I am within the rules of the House in speaking of it now. I wish to confute the statement of the Opposition that there was no menace, or
that we on this side of the House did not know anything about it, and I wish to confute it by the words of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark). The hon. member for Red Deer is a practical thinker, a philosopher, the very Cobden of the Opposition, and in Hansard, 1912-13, page 1200, volume 1, he says:
X personally am rather in a position to plume myself on this naval question.
So that he offers no apology for the opinion he gives.
The fact of the matter is that this German scare has become so attenuated a thing-
-if you please.
What date was that?
December 16, 1912.
That is some years ago.

The hon. gentleman
said:
The fact of the matter is that this German scare has become so attenuated a thing that it only finds a resting-place in such comparatively disordered minds as we have had an example of this afternoon.
And then the hon. gentleman spoke after recess, and during recess he does not seem to have considered the matter at all in the way of correcting it, for he says.
Mr. Speaker, when the. House rose at six o'clock X had pointed out that just as in the middle of the last century the French scare passed away without there having been the smell of gunpowder between the two great nations of France and Great Britain from that time, and as the Russian scare in the seventies passed away likewise without there hav-' ing been a trigger pulled then or since; so . happily for humanity and civilization the German scare of yesterday is vanishing. I think I shall be able to offer proof from the best possible sources that a generation from now we shall be looking back upon this scare as another of the human follies and upon the historical fact that following it there was not the firing of a shot by the one or the other of these two great Christian nations.
A little further on in the same speech he says:
There is no emergency. But the extraordinary political situation we are in in Canada is this: that although there is no emergency we have a government which comes cooly forward for its only naval policy with an emergency contribution.
Thus he confessed that the Government must have thought there was an emergency, must have thought that there was a reason for action, but he could tell them there was none. How disturbing it must be to mem-

bers of the Opposition these days, responsible and irresponsible, to think that they told us there was no menace and that we did not know anything about it, and that we did not know what we were doing, and that we were just as much in the dark as they.
May I ask a question?
Yes.

May I say that I ask the question with very great reluctance. I do not see the connection between what my hon. friend is saying and the tariff, but he has given me permission to ask a question, and it is this: If he and the Government he supports knew there was a menace, why did they for fourteen months sit on their oars and do nothing, after the Senate rejected the Dreadnought proposal?

Hear, hear.
IMr. BURNHAM: When the applause has died away, Mr. Speaker, I answer the question thus: It was because of the tremendous opposition which was offered by the Liberal party in this House and in the Senate; it was because of their lack of sympathy with the efforts being made by the Government; it was because we had been kept here the entire winter by the Liberals, who did not believe in doing anything in the circumstances. It is true that the menace has nothing to do with the tariff, but having spent forty-five minutes on the tariff I thought it was long enough, and that I would give you a treat by turning to something else. I find unfortunately that some don't appreciate my efforts in that direction. Let us refer for a moment to Imperialism, and I entirely agree with the Globe's stand in this particular. Here is what the Globe said in its issue of February 20th inst.:
Our imperialistic friends are now talking about rebuilding the Empire after the war. Has not the Empire just as it is proved reasonably efficient; why rebuild it?
That is what I say, hut I want to say more. The Naval Service Act of 1910, section 22, says:
The Governor in Council may place the naval forces, or any part thereof, on active service at any time that it appears advisable to do so, by reason of an emergency.
First of all, the Governor in Council may place the naval forces on active service, and I emphasize the word " may," and in the second place the Governor in Council can only do so if there is an emergency. So, if 
you prove there is no emergency, as in the present case of a war going on, you are in the soup, Mr. Speaker. We want it understood all the time that we belong to the Empire; that these forces are at the service of the Empire until such time as we say they are not; not as this Act, which says that they are not until we say they are. After that, if we want to meet and say that we cannot do this and that we cannot do that for various reasons, it is within our power to do so. That is consistent with the entire freedom and personal and practical independence of Canada. It is consistent with every ideal that we should like to have that we are managing our own affairs, but the proposition contained in the Naval Service Act is a practical declaration of independence.
Does the hon. member know that it is identical with the provisions of the Militia Act?
I have heard that certainly, but that does not defend it at all. If you think that is a confutation of my argument, you will have to think again.
The Militia Act was passed when a Conservative Government was in power.

The Conservatives may have made lots of mistakes, but they are trying to repair them. Section 23 says:
In case of an emergency the Governor in Council may place at the disposal of His Majesty-
That means that he has not done so as yet.
-for general service in the Royal Navy, the Naval Service or any part thereof, any ships or vessels of the Naval Service, and the officers and seamen serving in such ships or vessels, or any officers or seamen belonging to the Naval Service.
Section 24 says:
Whenever the Governor in Council places the Naval Service or any part thereof on active service, as provided in the two preceding sections, if Parliament is then separated by such adjournment or prorogation as will not expire with ten days, a proclamation shall issue for a meeting of Parliament within fifteen days, and Parliament shall accordingly meet and sit upon the day appointed by such proclamation, and shall continue to sit in like manner as if it had stood adjourned or prorogued to the same day.
There is the gist of the Liberal opposition to an Empire. You stand out until such times as you say you are in; and if it suits your interest and your prejudices and your meanness, you will say you belong to

the Empire and that you are under the old mother's wing; hut if it does not suit you, you can stay out, and you provide for that contingency by being out, so that, if it is going to be expensive and not going to serve your immediate purpose, if it is not going to be a good vote catching measure, why then you are out and you will not instruct the Governor in Council at all. He must be instructed by his advisors and he will not be instructed; or at least it will be long before he is and then Parliament will have to be called, and when Parliament has been called together, the Liberals will begin with their " ifs " and their " ands ". This is the Liberal idea of loyalty to the Empire. I am not in favour of Imperial federation. Imperial federation with a central council would mean the dismemberment of the Empire in a week. I do not believe in that at all. I believe in Canada remaining as she is at the present time without the Naval Service Act. Repeal the Naval Service Act.

That is what the Government promised to do and they did not do it. They did not dare to do it.
Mr. BURNllAM: They should have done it. I will concede that at any rate in my opinion.

Suppose the
Naval Service Act had been repealed, what would my hon. friend have done with the Rainbow and Niobe?

I would have taken the Rainbow and the Niobe and put them on the end of a toothpick and have presented them to the first passer-by.

The House resumed at eight o'clock.

I will not detain the House further at any length, but I wish to make a few further remarks to emphasize my observations on the subject of trade. There has been a serious misapprehension, I think, as to the doctrine laid down by Cobden. In the preface to an edition of his speeches, compiled by Thorold Rogers and John Bright, this observation is made, and it is one, I think, that should be borne in mind by those who severely criticise protection, especially with regard to the incidence of taxation:
He saw, for example, that no ultimate benefit would ensue to the mass of the people by the abolition of all taxes on food, unless what he called, by a pardonable metaphor, " free trade in la#id," were also established.
That, I think, is important, and has a very direct bearing, especially in the face of the somewhat violent attacks made upon the protective tariff with reference to food. Then, again, in this preface I find something of a still more profound nature, something that the protectionist particularly lays claim to have adopted as against the free trader who has absolutely defied it, and yet which is the foundation of Cobdenism:
A cautious student of political economy, he knew that this science, the difficulty of which he fully recognized, was, or ought to be, eminently inductive.
Now, free trade is founded wholly and solely upon a narrow a priori principle or statement, from which are deduced certain rules for the guidance of mankind. Free traders would make political economy the deductive science par excellence. As they expound it, political economy is not an inductive science; it pays no attention whatever to results, nor does it cite facts; but, beginning with a principle of free exchange, free labour-free everything-proceeds upon the belief that all else will follow. It is a good deal like the physicist with the Newtonian principle of gravitation, who, having solved that, looks for the explanation of everything else in the terms of this one great fact, except that it errs to begin with. But the protectionist looks to see what nature has afforded and what man has done, and seeks to apply the remedy from time to time applicable to the 9ases before him. It is useless to say that a certain principle must be assumed and that from that everything must proceed and that all mankind must conform, because it is this sort of thing that has landed free traders in such a pit of distress, and it is that which has left them without a single companion in the world except in Great Britain.
I find in one of Cobden's speeches, something that shows exactly what he meant when he advocated the abolition of the Corn Laws. He shows that the whole bearing of that agitation which resulted in the mighty revolution inaugurated by Sir Robert Peel and brought about by him was altogether relative to the prosperity of the manufacturers:
If I know anything, it means-
That is, the abolition of the Corn Laws means
-increased trade, and the claim of a right besides to exchange our manufactures with the corn of all other countries, by which we should very much increase the extent of our trade.
That, I submit, is the real basis of Cobdenism-an attempt to develop manufactur-

ing in Britain. On the abolition of the Corn Laws, with more cheaply fed labour, and, as I said before, with patent rights and a monopoly of inventions, Great Britain sprang into that pre-eminence which she enjoys to-day and which is represented by the capitalist manufacturer. Britain, to-day is represented in her immense wealth and power by the British manufacturer, and he owes his success to the prescience of Cobden who saw that England was too small to give free scope to her own powers of food production, and saw likewise that landlords were living in idleness upon a monopoly, and who said:	Do away with
these things and you will raise manufacture to tremendous prominence-and he succeeded in doing it.
I wish to refer for a moment also to a well-known newspaper published in Ottawa 

the Citizen-because of its attack upon the Budget. It says that our system of taxation showed last year that we were willing to pay $25,000,000 in taxes rather than let the work go to Great Britain. This newspaper, I frankly admit, is a journal of great influence and superior tone; although it indulges in the luxury of contradicting itself from time to time as the different writers present their views to the public. Its idea of prosperity, however, seems to be to send the work that we ought to do in Canada somewhere else. It says that we have penalized ourselves. Well, if we had the work, and kept the money fix the country, and paid the taxes into our own treasury, it is difficult to see where we have penalized ourselves. We may have penalized some people, some class in the country, but we cannot have penalized Canada as a whole. Therefore, I deprecate these reckless statements in these influential newspapers. They convey a wrong impression and mislead the unthinking public.
* The Citizen seems to he betrayed by catchwords-many good men are betrayed by catch-words. The catch-words to which I refer in this case are these: " Buy in the cheapest market and sell in the dearest."
It seems to be the impression that the typical free trader all his life dwells in a free trade terrestrial paradise and goes round chuckling over the fact that he bought in the cheapest market and sold in the dearest. That is the whole and soul of liberalism, to buy in the cheapest market and sell in the dearest, a principle which in itself is a manifest absurdity because economically if you continue to buy in the cheapest and sell in the dearest market how is the cheapest market going to pay for the goods in the long run? It can-

not be done, it is an impossibility, but as a catch word it is all right to those influenced by unnatural cupidity and to stay public criticism, while the moneyed man bags the market. It also appeals to a certain class of labour men who have not in the past had time to investigate, but who are now getting shorter hours under protection and are looking into the matter and seeing the falsity of this system. Free trade therefore is pre-eminently a doctrine of selfishness. It says: " Laissez faire, laissez passer, laissez aller, pay attention to nothing." Once a capitalist has got his money, then you have put the whole world in his power. Tou have made the only legal tender that which he possesses in abundance, and you ask him or he asks you to let everything else go just step to the one side and you will see the greatest fight you ever saw in your life. That is exactly what happens. He has the world at his finger tips, he is the master of the world, and therefore it is, I submit, pre-eminently a doctrine of selfishness. It reminds one a good deal of the case of "Lo, the poor Indian." The Indian brings in four beaver skins and trades them for a plug of tobacco. That is free trade. The capitalist is the man who furnishes the tobacco and his unsuspecting victim is the man who pays the four beaver skins. He has commanded, by reason of his superior acumen and capital, the immense labour of the poor Indian, who has probably journeyed hundreds of miles and sat up many nights to gain these beaver skins to buy his little plug of tobacco. The idea of letting the strong alone, the idea of inviting the strong to take care of the weak, the idea of putting the weaker part of the world in the custody of the strong on an economic non-sentimental basis and expecting them to be taken care of, is in itself an absurdity; you might just as well ask vice to take care of virtue. The truth of the matter is that the principle of control should govern and, in so far as protection means control, protection is good, but in so far as it means handing a monopoly to anybody, or an inequitable system of exchange, production or employment, it is of course absolutely bad.
I wish to refer briefly to the new cry of " Made in Canada," a most admirable motto for any people, the substitution of a request for a law. We ask the people of the country, although they may have established trade with other countries, to remember Canada, the land where they have been prosperous and happy, the land^ of noble

prospects, of health, prosperity and above all, the land of home. We ask them to remember that and not to sell their souls and their love of Canada for a little money; we ask them to remember, and rather than go outside of Canada, to be prepared to pay a greater labour cost for an article. It will come back to them, even on that low ground, but apart from that, let us remember that we cannot make of this country anything except by co-operation and consideration. We must remember that to keep the work in the country must be our supreme aim and object, and if we do not do that, ihow can we expect to make this country great? Let us be an independent, industrial Canada, let us feel and know that if the whole world was excluded, if there was a wall fifty feet high around Canada, that we ourselves, with our resources, our capabilities, our population, could go on and thrive, interchanging our products one. with the other, and so securing a prosperity that would be tantamount, to perfection and absolute balance. So much so indeed that it calls to mind a fact laid down and descanted upon by many economists, that foreign trade is a trap which beguiles people into the idea that they are extending their prosperity, whereas in the last analysis foreign trade should not exist because every country should manufacture and grow and produce for itself; every individual should have inherent in him the same quality. The minute the process is reversed and the individual extends out of himself, he makes himself depend on somebody else, he loses his free condition and becomes another man; the nation becomes another nation and becomes unsettled; labour becomes unsettled, and the whole involved system of exchange and interchange exposes the people of the country to the machinations of the unprincipled.
A great deal of the trouble arises, of course, from the altogether false position of gold. Gold, of course, is nothing more than wool .or timber or fish or beef. It so happens that, being a hanay thing to carry about and being universally appreciated, it is chosen as the one thing which will satisfy all parties and is used as a medium of exchange; but because of that there is attached to it a natural monopoly, and though we may have any quantity of timber, any quantity of wool, any quantity of mutton or of cattle, we can do nothing with them if people do not come along with the cash to enable us to transfer the products that we have to some other place. If they
do not they will remain where they are forever, or so long as they do not rot, showing that the placing of one commodity, namely gold, in such a pre-eminent and monopolistic position is wrong, it is dangerous, it is serious and it is the cause unquestionably of a great deal of our unhappiness.
Strange to say, it has been customary, for what reason I do not understand, to laugh and sneer at the balance of trade. You would think the balance of trade was some bogey or absurdity that was in the imagination of the ignorant and unlettered. We are told time and again that the balance of trade is against England or against France or against so and so, and that is followed by a peal of loud, reverberating laughter, and the fears of a place like Canada are supposed to be at once stilled. Of course that is an absolutely unfair, improper and incorrect statement of the balance of trade. The balance of trade, because of the use of the word trade, is made to refer to the exports and imports of commodities, whereas it properly refers to all the transactions that a country has- cash, goods, means of transportation and everything else; and we find that the balance of trade so far from being against England and France is, on account of the foreign interest that they receive, and on account of transportation and other things, immeas-ureably in their favour. This laughing at the balance of trade has a bad effect, for the people are lulled into a false sense of security. The balance of trade in its narrower and moie restricted meaning, referring to commodities, shows one thing; and that is, that unless the balance of trade in commodities is in your favour you are on the high road to immediate ruin. The capital which has given strength and pre-eminence to the nations to which I have referred was amassed by reason of the balance of trade in commodities being so long in their favour. If the United States continues to have a balance of trade of hundreds of millions m its favour against Canada, it is easily within our imaginations to grasp that the United States must be laying up a great store of prosperity and profit at our expense; and we must pay them for these things by borrowing money from England, and exhaust our resources in paying foreign interest. Is it any wonder then that the cry is raised from day to day, that our taxes are tiemendous and that our borrowing powers seem to be without limit? That is one of the peculiarities of the preference. We were told by an hon. gentleman yesterday that the preference
41G

enabled us to borrow more money from England, and yet the very same gentleman told us that thi-s country was going to perdition because of its extravagance in borrowing-another nail in the coffin of preference. Therefore, it seems to me that Finance Ministers in making up their annual budgets might very well give for the information of the people a complete analysis of all the receipts and liabilities of the nation so that we should know exactly how we stand.
