Then we should see that although the balance of trade was in our favour with respect to commodities and production, actually it would be vastly against us when we took into account the foreign interest that we pay and the other liabilities; and we should see that our resources would be ultimately exhausted if we did not do our own work in Canada. If we send the money and the profit out of this country we'are bound to pay for it in the long run.
I wish to make one more reference before closing, and that is to what I may call the ethical standard of the present day. In that connection I wish to say that trades unions exist for the purpose of curbing internationalism, and controlling the labour market. Except by force, there can be no trades union, logically speaking, in a country that has free trade and free labour competition. Agriculture is of course in the same predicament. It is customary to say that agriculture is not of a manufacturing character; but as a matter of fact the farmer is a manufacturer. He puts his labour into the soil and gets it out again, and is just as much a manufacturer as the man who makes lumber out of timber or digs minerals and makes them into something else. I have often thought how profoundly true was the remark made by the right hon. leader of the Opposition in an address to -a large assembly of farmers near Toronto some three years ago. In discussing the conditions best suited to the farmer and their prospects for better trade and a superior development, the right hon. gentleman said: "Your best market is the home market." That is how he was reported in the Globe. I cut it out and have	treasured it ever	since.He	laid	particular emphasis on
that fact , and I admired the candour of the right hon. gentleman as much as the fact itself. He laid it down to the farmers that the home market was pre-eminently the best, and I am sure the Ontario farmer knows, now that he has the competition of the West, that without the home market he would be a ruined man.
In the old days people got along very

well without money. When they had anything to trade, they lugged it around to their neighbours until they got what they wanted in exchange. It occurred to a princess in the kingdom of Lydia that it would be a good idea to earmark the gifts to the goddesses in the temples, especially gold which was particularly an Asiatic product. The idea was good, because the ear mark not only indicated where the gifts came from, but was a guarantee of genuineness and from that sprang the idea of earmarking money. First of all, it had oniy a few earmarks such as a seal or mark of some peculiar weapon carried by an Asiatic prince. By-and-by the designs became more elaborate until finally the head of the Sovereign was used. As soon as that occurred and money became money, the financiers proceeded tr invent the science of money, and capitalists ever since have been dealing in it, not always I am sure to the advantage of those who in all other walks of life are absolutely dependent upon it. Cash money is at the outside only one-fiftieth of the wealth of the whole world. It would be impossible to transport cash in payment for all the goods bought, because in a very short time the country that did so would be left without any cash, and would be on its beam ends. So the system of bills of exchange was adopted, which is a good deal like our system of a clearing house for banks. This was necessary because no nation in the world would allow its gold reserve to sink below a certain level; and in times of war when distress is greatest nations take particular care that the gold reserve in the treasury is as big as possible; for it is admitted that the country that has most gold will win the fight.
In Greece, the ideal was superiority. She gave to the world great sculptors, great painters, tragedians, great writers of tragedies and comedies, great orators such as Demosthenes, and so on. All the countries together in the world have never produced their equal since for quality or quantity. Why? Because the Greeks were a highly imaginative and intellectual people. Their ideal was typified in the reward they gave to their great athletes at the Olympian games. The winners were crowned with a simple chaplet of wild olive, the olive tree being typical of Greece. Money they never dreamt of, gold they despised, and a rich man they suspected.
Nowhere, even in Homeric history, is there any reference to the riches of anybody. It is their fighting ability, or their eloquence.

or beauty or strength that is spoken of, but never their riches. It has remained for this age to glorify the idea of materialism as typified by the rich man.
I wish, therefore, in conclusion, to say that every one of us must realize that we have sold ourselves very largely to materialism, whereas in this age we should keep constantly before ourselves the Christian or ethical ideal as opposed to the materialistic ideal. But Christianity is practically at a discount, or, if not at a discount, it occupies an altogether secondary position in its influence. It is not prominent, it is not predominant, its ideals aTe laughed iat, and theology occupies about as much of a place in the public mind as political economy. What the people want is money, and it is very easy to glide from the wish for or want of capital into desiring to get it at any price and at the sacrifice of any principle. We see every day the mergers in this country, we see the banks that have gone up, we see the investigations, the disclosures, the horrible catas-trophies from time to time that are taking place. We see them increasing, and we see people vainly endeavouring to stem this tide of corruption by laws. It can not be done, Mr. Speaker. There are laws enough on the statute books to send all the people in the country to jail. Unless the people become good enough to do more without law, to rise superior to laws, the ideal of a nobler human being will never succeed in placing itself spiritually and ethically on that high plane which it ought to occupy in our minds, and where it would be worthy of those great Greek idealists who have so long preceded us.

I think it will be conceded by everybody in this House, and also out of the House, that the propositions submitted by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. White) in his Budget speech are amongst the most important that have ever been submitted to this House. He comes to Parliament, as is usual, for the supply of money for the coming year, and the money he asks for is for the ordinary expenses of the country and for the continuance of the war. The money that he asks for naturally divides itself into two parts-that part that he asks for in connection with the war, and that part that he asks for in connection with the ordinary expenses of the country. I will, for a moment or two, deal with that portion of his Budget that asks for money in connection with the war. I want to say to my hon. friend that with reference to everything that he asks this House to vote in 27
connection with the carrying on of the war, he will have every man on this side of the House right behind him; we will support him to the limit, and vote anything that he says is necessary for the carrying on of this war. This war has been forced on Great Britain, and the other portions of the Empire. It is not of their own seeking. Great Britain has gone to war for self-preservation in one sense, and for the purpose of seeing that smaller nations are allowed to live and that treaties are kept.
When the war broke out the Government that happened to be in power at the time took, in my judgment, the proper and necessary steps. They called a special session of Parliament and asked for $50,000,000, which was voted without a word of criticism on this side. Now, they are asking for $100,000,000,	and we propose	to
vote that without a word of criticism from this side.	We think that the
Government took the proper course and that they are doing all right in carrying on the war and we say that Canada is with Great Britain in this war to the extent of her men and	her	money. If	my	hon.friend the Minister of Finance should find out at the end of the next fiscal year, March 31, 1916, that the $100,000,000 that he is	asking for	to-day isnot sufficient	for	the war,	the	voteshall be supplemented, all he has to do is to come before Parliament and ask for what is necessary and he will find that every Liberal,	and	I am satisfied	every
Conservative, in fact every man, will be right behind any proposition he makes and will not criticise the amount he asks for.
We naturally reserve to ourselves the right to expect that it shall be properly expended and to ask, if it is not properly expended, that the matter shall be looked into. I do not imagine for a moment that any Minister of Militia or any Government can look after every dollar of expenditure and see that everything is done rightly. We expect there will be mistakes, that there will be a certain amount of wrong-doing that the Government cannot stop, but whenever there is any very persistent course of wrong-doing, where contractors are charging two prices or contractors are putting in an inferior class of goods for our soldiers, we reserve the right to ask for an investigation of these matters. I think it is our duty to ourselves and to the country and I am satisfied that it is our duty to the Government and that the Government will be a great deal better in the end if matters are looked into and stopped in the beginning



instead of being allowed to run on for a year or two or to the extent of the duration [DOT] of the war. I do not think I need refer any further to that phase of the question.
We come now to consider that portion of my hon. friend's Budget which deals with the money required for the ordinary expenditure of the country and for the capital account expenditure. While we do not criticise the other portion of the Budget I feel that we are absolutely justified in thoroughly criticising that portion of the Budget where my hon. friend the Minister of Finance is asking for money to carry on the ordinary work of the country. It is just as much our duty and right to criticise and look into this matter at this session as at any other session that has ever been held. I think it is more necessary because we are in a very peculiar position at this time. We find that the country is in a most depressed condition, not on account of the war altogether. It may have had something to do with it, but the depression was on the country, conditions were bad, imports were falling, everything was largely at a standstill, the business of the country was going back day by day, month by month, year by year, and in face of all this the Minister of Finance comes down to this House and asks for a greater Budget than ever has been asked for in the history of Canada. My hon. friend tells us that his expenditures are going up so much and therefore he must have more revenue. There are two ways to equalize revenue and expenditure. One way is to do as my friend the Minister of Finance has attempted to do, increase the- revenue; another way is to decrease the expenditure. What is the better way, what is the sensible way, in what way would any common-sense man go about equalizing revenue and expenditure? Would it be in hard times to try to collect more taxes or would it be to take the common-sense view and reduce expenditure?
The Minister of Finance is a business man, and I venture to say if he had been allowed a free hand he would never have submitted such a Budget. No business man in Canada, no business man in the civilized world, under the conditions that obtain at present in the Dominion, would have come down with a proposal asking for an expenditure of $190,000,000, apart from the cost of the war, when he admits that the revenue will be about $120,000,000. And yet, that is what he has done. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Mac-[Mr. Turriff.J
lean) suggested that the expenditure should have been cut down, and I say without the slightest fear of successful contradiction that the expenditure could have been cut down, with the full consent of the people of Canada, to meet the revenue of 1915-16, which will be $120,000,000, and that is some $30,000,000 greater than the expenditure was in Canada when the present Government came into power three and a half years ago. There is absolutely no reason on earth for this great increase of expenditure, from $87,000,000 in 1911 to $140,000,000 at the present time. Suppose the Minister of Finance had submitted a ballot to every voter in Canada, asking: Are you in favour of reducing the public expenditure by $30,000,000 or are you in favour of raising that $30,000,000 partly by a direct tax and partly by the raising of the customs duties by which for every dollar you put into the treasury you put three dollars into the pockets of the manufacturers, how many of the voti rs of Canada do you think would have marked tnat ballot -against reducing expenditures? It is the people of Canada, who have the right to say whether expenditures shall be reduced or taxes increased.
Let us go to the people and find out.

You cannot go to the people too quick for me. Gentlemep on tne other side of the House and their friends outside have been threatening us that if we do not behave ourselves and be good boys and keep quiet, they will dissolve the House and go to the country. I would tell these gentlemen that in view of this Budget they can dissolve the House if they dare and appeal to the people. My hon. friend from. Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) and the gentleman who sits beside him (Mr. Meighen) will have a good deal to explain when they go out to the western farmers.
It will not be hard.
My hon. friend will have a good deal to explain, and he will have to use greater efforts than he did before to secure a majority.
There will be others.
On that side of the House.

I think I am looking at a good many hon. gentlemen opposite to whom the remarks of my hon. friend will apply. The Minister of Public Works said yesterday that he hoped there would be no election. I venture to think that there is not

a man on the other side of the House who does not know what to take out of that assertion. I notice that while the Minister of Public Works says he hopes there is not going to be an election until after the war, that he is mighty busy, and hon. gentlemen opposite are mighty busy, sending out party literature at the present moment.

That is the way they
keep the truce.

I can assure my hon.
friends opposite, that we, as well as they, know how to interpret the smooth words of the Minister of Public Works. We know the Minister of Public Works and we are not blinded one iota by anything he says about deferring the election. My hon. friend stated that when the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) was referring to cutting down expenditures, he did not show how this extra revenue that is needed could be raised if taxes were not levied. That is true, but the hon. member pointed out that it was not necessary to raise this extra revenue at all if the expenditure were cut down. My hon. friend asked if we would stop the public works in view of the fact that there is a great deal of unemployment in the country, but I ask him, who supplies the money for carrying on public works? It is the taxes paid by the people of Canada that provides that money. If the Minister of Finance spends $30,000,000 more this year than he needs to, it is the people of Canada who will have to supply that money, and I tell the Government that when they say they are benefiting the people of Canada by carrying on public- works, they are simply taking the money out of one pocket of the ratepayers of Canada and putting it into another. I say that the expenditure on public works could be cut in two and the good of the country would not suffer to the extent of one dollar.
The hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Mac-donell) took great credit to himself and to the Government of which he is a supporter that in the Estimates for public works this coming year there is a reduction of about $11,000,000 over the estimate of last year. But let me tell the hon. member that last year the Minister of Public Works put in an estimate of $.'13,000,000, not that he had the slightest intention of spending $33,000,000, but to hang it out as a bribe to the different constituencies of Canada, and for no other purpose. The Minister of Public Works did not spend that money and he had no idea of spending it when he put it in the Estimates. But, neverthless, when the Minister 274
of Public Works comes forward now and asks for $11,000,000 less than he did in the inflated estimates of last year, the hon. gentleman from Toronto points to what an economical government we have. What my hon. friend is asking for now is double what was expected on public works when his party came into power three years ago.
Is my hon. friend finding fault with the Minister of Public Works for not expending the whole of last year's vote?

Certainly not. The sums were put in the Estimates of last year, not for the purpose of expending all of them, but as a bribe to the different,constituencies in case of an election and as nothing else. That is what I said, and that is what I stand by.
There was no election.

There was always the
prospect of an election last fall, and it would have looked very well to go through the different constituencies and say:	See
what this Government has done; it has voted tens of thousands and hundreds of thousands of dollars for public works. But the money was not expended, and this year my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works is asking for more than his expenditure of last year. Is it a time to go in for lavish expenditures when the revenue is falling away tremendously, and when my hon. friend the Minister of Finance has to borrow every dollar required for the war, every dollar for expenditure for public works on capital account, and, if he had not put on extra taxation, a considerable part of the ordinary expenditure on consolidated account?
What does the common-sense business man do when his revenue is partly cut off? Let us take the case of a workingman who for the last ten years until a year ago has been earning $2.50 a day. He is an industrious man and has an economical wife. He buys a lot on the outskirts of the city and builds a little house. As the years go by his house becomes worth say $4,000 to $5,000. Suddenly there comes depressed times throughout the Dominion, and he finds that instead of his wages being $2.50 a day they are cut down to $1.50 a day. What does he do if he is sensible and has succeeded, as the man I speak of has? Does he go to a loan company and borrow enough money to enable him to continue living at the rate of $2.50 a day, or does he cut his

living expenses from $2.50 to $1.50 a day? The latter is what the common-sense artisan does on every occasion.
Let me give my hon. friend the Minister of Finance another instance that will appeal more to him. As I said a moment ago, my hon. friend the Minister of Finance is a business man first and foremost, and moreover, he is a good business man when he is left alone-a first-class business man. Formerly, he was always able to conduct his business in a good and prosperous way, never making his expenditures greater than his revenue. It is only when he is Minister of Finance in the company in which he finds himself that he is reduced to borrowing.
Inefficient.

Supposing my hon. friend the Minister of Finance was the president of a company that for years past had been earning 8 per cent on its capital and had been paying an annual dividend of 6 per cent. As the years went on it gathered a nice rest account to give stability to the company to tide over any difficult time.
When hard times come along, 9 p.m. such as we are now experiencing, and the earnings of that company are reduced from 8 per cent to 5 per cent per annum, what would my hon. friend do? Would he continue to pay a dividend of 6 per cent if he saw hard times looming ahead with no prospect of better times for years to come, drawing out of the reserve account for it, and then, when the reserve account was eaten up, going to the banks and mortgaging the securities of his company to get money to continue paying that 6 per cent? Would he keep up the expenditure? Not for one moment. Would my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, countenance such a procedure; and if his board of directors insisted upon keeping up the expenditure he would resign the presidency of that company, just as any sensible man would do. If that is good business for an individual, industrial or financial company, why should it not be good business for the Dominion of Canada? The ministers of this Government are simply directors and the people of Canada shareholders, and the ministers should be actuated by the same principles and standards of honour and honesty in expenditure and revenue as the president and directors of any financial or industrial company. But have they been actuated by such priciples? No. We find the country brought to a state of depression by the extravagance of this

Government to a large extent; and instead of curtailing expenditure, my hon. friend says: No, clap on full sail; spend all the money you like on public works; spend all the money you like on all the other departments; and, although we have to mortgage the resources of this country, we will expend all the money that is -wanted. Is that a common-sense business view to take? Is that a common-sense way in which to handle the finances of this country? It is the very worst kind of financing that has ever been attempted in this country from Confederation down to the present time. If this proposition of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance is made law in its present state, it will be the heaviest blow that has been given to the development and prosperity of Canada since Confederation, and it will take Canada many a long year to recover from the effects of it-.
Cheer up.

I am usually of a somewhat optimistic nature. I generally look at the bright side of things, and I would particularly like to be able to look at the bright side of this question to-night; but I certainly see that we are to be in for a long period of depression. It cannot be helped. Our main customers on the continent of Europe will not be in a good position to buy from us when this war is Over. We shall not be able to produce so as to sell to those countries as cheaply as in the past. Why? Because of the act of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance in heaping burdens upon the backs of the farmers.
Terrible!
My hon. friend is right. He does not strike the nail on the head very often, but he has hit it right this time.
I want to correct my hon. friend. I did not say "tariff "; I said " terrible."

All right. The Minister of Finance tells the House and the country that a part of this taxation that he proposes to put on is a war tax-that it is a tax to help out the war. I say this Government is deliberately making an attempt to get money from the people under false pretenses. Not a dollar of what the minister proposes to raise by direct taxation or by the increased tariff duties is for the purposes of the war. I give the Minister of Finance and the members of the Government generally credit for this-that they have made the people of Canada to a certain extent believe

that this money is for the war. But I can tell them that, when the people of Canada realize that there is not a word of truth in the representations that they have made on this subject, when they realize that the Minister of Finance is borrowing all the money for the war and that all he has collected by taxation is to enable the Government to continue its course of reckless extravagance, the Government will not last five minutes after that question has, been fairly submitted to a vote of the people. It takes a good deal of work, a good deal of explanation by the newspapers and public men to get the facts home to the people. But they will learn it. They will learn that the increased taxation is raising the cost of living, and God knows it was high enough. But it is going to be higher because this Government taxes practically everything the poor man eats or wears. The people will understand that before long, because each man will feel it in his pocket. Every time a postcard is mailed there is a special tax of one cent- the cost is doubled. Every time a letter is mailed, a stamp printed " war tax " must be put on at the cost of an additional cent.
I wonder at the Government having the nerve to call this a war tax when they know it is nothing of the kind. If the Minister of Finance wanted to be exactly fair with the people of Canada, if he wanted the people to understand the reason for putting on the stamp marked " war tax " on each letter posted, he would proceed in a different way; in each post office there should be a little box, and when any person wished to mail a letter, instead of putting on the additional stamp, he would drop one cent in the box and on that box would be the inscription: " For two poor men: subscription for Mackenzie and Mann." How long would the people of Canada stand for a tax of that kind? And the same should be done in the case of every railway ticket or steamship ticket bought, every cheque going through a bank, every bill of exchange drawn-" For two poor men: Bill and Dan."
The Minister of Finance made the statement that he expected to get $8,000,000 or $10,000,000 out of the war taxes. What does he want it for? He wants it for the general revenue purposes of the country to pay back the money that the Government has given, during the past year, illegally to Mackenzie and Mann. Because we, a year ago in this Parliament, guaranteed $45,000,000 in bonds in the interest of these people, did that give the Government the right to hand over twelve and a half millions to Mackenzie and Mann? Why, the Minister of Finance
had no more right to hand over that money to Mackenzie and Mann than he had to give it to me or to give it to the first man he may meet on leaving this House. If the directors of a financial corporation had done such a thing, it would not be long before they would be cross-eyed looking out through iron bars. My information is that every minister in the Government is liable to impeachment for that very thing. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance will have to come down to this House and get remedial legislation to legalize that illegal transaction of handing over the money of the people of Canada to Mackenzie and Mann and the Grand Trunk Pacific. That is the exact state of the case-I am not overstating it by a hair's breadth; and no one knows that better than the Minister of Finance.
So that this, instead of being a direct tax for the war as the Government is trying dishonestly to make out, is a tax that Mackenzie and Mann have more interest in than anybody else, because they will get the greatest share of it-in fact, they have it already. The Government have the glad hand and the warm heart for the big railway corporations and the big manufacturers, because there are fat election subscriptions to be secured. But for the workingman and the farmer there is the cold hand: " What do you want? We will give you a seven and a half per cent increased duty. That is good enough for you. Go back to your work, and produce more. Patriotism and production."

Will the hon. gentleman kindly let us know' what he thinks of the argument of his friend the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) that we should not have taxed bituminous coal because that tax is too hard on the railways?

I will say to my hon. and hair-splitting friend that if he will wait for a few minutes and, when I get through the few remarks I have to make, will ask me that question or any other, I will endeavour, to the best of my poor ability, to give him an answer-and I have no doubt that I shall be able to give him an answer that will not be satisfactory to him.
There is the position that we are in. The Minister of Finance comes to the people of Canada, and says: We want you to give us , some twenty-two to twenty-five millions of extra taxes, and so we propose to raise the duties. It was well pointed out by my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) last

night-and the idea had not occurred to me, 1 am free to confess, and had not occurred to a good many members on either side of the House-that last August, in the extra session, the Minister of Finance put on extra taxes. I do not remember at what he estimated them, but I think it was about $15,000,000 a year. I would ask the Finance1 Minister whether that estimate has been borne out. I imagine it would be much better borne out than his expectations of revenue from the tariff he is now putting on, simply because so much of it came from sugar, whisky and tobacco.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I stated in the Budget speech that the effect of the increase of August last had been to counteract the decrease which would otherwise have taken place in excise, but that until the end of the year it is impossible to state with any degree of accuracy what the precise effect of the changes of last August will be. The amount received will, in my judgment, owing to the very great interruption of general business last fall on account of the war, be less than I estimated.

I thank the minister for the information; it is about as I would expect. Trade has not been good and it was to be expected that the revenue received would be somewhat less than any man would have been justified in estimating at that time. If that has occurred in connection with the taxes that were imposed last August then I am afraid that the Minister of Finance will fall very much short in his estimate of extra revenue from the taxes he is about to impose. There is a certain limit to which you can go in the raising of revenue from taxes by tariff. That limit, I think, has been reached and more than reached by the extra taxes now being imposed. If any judgment had been used in selecting certain articles which might bear the taxes, probably some extra revenue would have been received; but when you put on a horizontal tax, raising the tariff on everything without rhyme or reason, you are bound in many cases to put the tariff so high that instead of increasing the revenue you are bound to decrease it. I remember very well the discussion that took place a year or two ago, when the Minister of Finance cut the duty on cement. It was pointed out that the duty on cement was approximately 60 per cent ad valorem. Afterwards my hon. friend put the duty on cement back where it was and it has remained there ever since. Now my hon.
(Mr. Turriff.]
friend comes forward and puts an extra duty of 71 per cent on cement. Does any hon. gentleman on the other side of the House think for one moment that we are going to continue importing cement under these circumstances? This extra duty practically cuts out the importation of cement into Canada. How much revenue will it put into the treasury? The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) last night pointed out how much revenue had been received for duty on cement. The minister in putting extra duties on cement is not going to receive even the amount of revenue that is now being derived from that source. He is cutting off the revenue from cement altogether, and to whom has he given it? Is he saving it to the farmer or to the town or villages that are using cement for paving, or to the business man who uses cement in putting up buildings? Is he saving it to any user of cement? No, Mr. Speaker, he is not, he is handing over a bonus of thousands and hundreds of of thousands of dollars to the greatest combine and merger that we have in Canada to-day. Not a dollar of increased revenue, but thousands of dollars of increased cost for the user of cement and increased profits for the cement merger. Will my hon. friend or the hon. member from South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell), who said last night that those who are able to pay are being taxed, that the big interests are being taxed, tell me how much the cement merger is paying of this tax? I do not think anybody will attempt to answer that question.
You had better guess it, you have been guessing a lot.
My hon. friend was guessing all last night. He sat down guessing. My hon. friend was speaking for the manufacturers. He said he was a-
No my hon. friend is quite mistaken, and I do not think it is fair that he should say that. I did not say that or anything to that effect. I said I was a staunch protectionist.

A strong protectionist,
yes. If that does not mean the same thing I do not know what it means. However, I . take hack the expression I used as I certainly would not wish to put wrong words in the mouth of my hon. friend; but I would ask my hon. friend the minister or my hon. friend from South Toronto how much the cement merger is being taxed in this direct tax. Every poor man who sends $5 home to

his wife in the Old Country has to put a stamp on his cheque and another on the envelope which carries it. The poor man has to pay. But does the cement merger pay? The man who sends a |5 cheque home to his mother in the Old Country pays exactly the same to carry that cheque and the same amount on that cheque as the cement merger or any other merger pays on a cheque for $250,000 for raw material or for anything else they purchase. That is treating everybody alike in a sense, but it is not making the man who has the money pay in proportion, it is putting the burden on the poor man and letting the rich man go free. As I said a moment ago, let the thing once come home to the people of Canada, let them once realize the position, and they will take care of my hon. friends across the floor of the House.
Hear, hear; they will.

I have spoken of decreasing the public expenditure. I said that public works could be cut down. What about the officials in Canada? My hon. Mend from South Toronto last night asked my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) if he would be willing to cut down the civil service. Well, speaking for myself, I am prepared to answer that question, and I would say by all means cut down the Civil Service.
What percentage?
I was a civil servant myself a good many years here in Ottawa-

Hear, hear.
Mr. TURRIFFand I know something about the Civil Service. I know that when this Government came into power and when the old Government went out of power, the Civil Service was not undermanned to any extent. The Civil Service has never been undermanned in Canada, no matter which party was in power. Since my hon. friends opposite came into power they have dismissed some 2,000 odd, and they have taken on 10,500 up to a year ago, practically a difference of 8,000; and if the figures were brought up to date, the difference would probably be about 10,000. Are we doing any more work than we were three and a half yeaTs ago? The extra civil servants are not the only matter of expense. The other day I moved for a return as to the number of buildings rented by this Government since it came into power. The figures for Ottawa alone show that some $202,000 has been spent in rent
for offices to house these extra civil servants who were not required and are not required to-day. You cannot put on civil servants for less than $1,000 apiece per annum; and 10,000 civil servants at that rate mean $10,000,000 per annum. I say that the Civil Service could be cut down to what it was three and a half years ago, or even a great deal less than that, and the public service of Canada would not suffer to the extent of a five cent piece. So that if my hon. friend had wanted to cut down expenses, there was one way in which it could have been done. Take the public buildings being erected all over the country. I have looked through the Estimates, and I see that building after building costing $10,000, $20,000, $30,000 or $35,000 is being erected in places with less than 300 inhabitants.
Where?
All through Saskatchewan, Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.
Whereabouts in Prince Edward Island?

Let my hon. friend look at the Estimates; no doubt he has them in his desk. He will find the figures there. I say that a saving of $10,000,000 could be made in this direction without the public suffering in the slightest degree. I do not say that the present Government is much more to blame than the old one. Time after time, when our own party was in power, I endeavoured to shut off these expenditures on public buildings in different places.
Not in Parliament.
Yes.
Have you your "Hansard" with you?

My hon- friend can find it in "Hansard" I advocated it both in the House and out of it. Take the Post Office Department for example. A small town wants a public building, and the Government puts one up at a cost for lot and building of say $25,000. When the building is UPj you have to pay interest on that money for all time to come; you have to heat the building and put in a caretaker, and you have a continual stream of repairs, as any one can see by looking at the Estimates. The building has to be kept in repair even from the time it is built, and will cost altogether about $3,000 a year. I have in my own constituency two post offices which are not in public buildings, but the accommodation given to the public is equal to that

provided in the city of Ottawa, or in Montreal or Toronto or in any other place in the Dominion. The buildings are of solid brick, of first-class workmanship, perfectly heated, and have tables and chairs and pens and ink for the use of the public. A farmer can come in five miles and get his letter, sit down in the post office and answer it, and I will venture to say that the rent does not amount to $600 a year-not $2,000 or $3,000. Does any one suggest that either of those towns are suffering because they have not a public building for a post office? Not for a moment. The time has come when this Dominion-I do not mean this as a reflection on hon. gentlemen opposite more than on ourselves-but I say the time has coma when we have got to get down to brass tacks in the matter of expenditure. We cannot go on as we have been doing for the last twenty-five years. It simply cannot be done. The Finance Minister stated the other day that the fixed charges for interest next year would be $21,500,000, if I remember correctly. When my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition came into power in 1896, the fixed charges for interest were some $10,000,000. When he went out of power in 1911 the fixed interest charges were in round figures $12,000,000, representing an increase of $2,000,000 in about sixteen years. -When my hon. friends came into power three and a half years ago the fixed interest charges were $12,000,000, and next year the Finance Minister tells us that they will be $20,500,000, or an increase of $8,500,000. The Finance Minister of course is not responsible for the increase caused by our borrowings on account of the war. He is not to blame for that any more than we are. But the interest on our borrowings on account of the war will not make up that $8,500,000, and to that extent the Finance Minister is responsible.	.
I say we have come to a time when there must be retrenchment. When is it going to begin? Should it not begin now? Dues my hon. friend the Minister of Finance think he is going to make prosperity by taxing the people of Canada? It is absurd to think that he can bring about prosperity by simply putting his hands in the pockets of the people and taking out the money, and the sooner the Government realize the position that Canada is in, the better it will be for the people of this country. We must make a change. We must live more economically. We must spend less money. How can we spend less money and do the least injury to the public service? We could reduce the number 
of officials, reduce them largely, and not interfere with the public service. We could cut the cost of public works in two and not interfere with the public service. My hon. friend from South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) was very anxious last night .to know whether my hon. frierid from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) was willing to see the expenditure on Halifax cut down. I understand that they are spending some $15,000,000 or $20,000,000 in Halifax. I venture the assertion that if the money was properly expended you could do all that is necessary for the development of trade in the city of Halifax for $5,000,000 instead of $2o,000,000, and I venture the further assertion that the city of Halifax under the present circumstances would be perfectly willing to accept their share of reduction until conditions are better and the people of this country have more money and until there is not so great a discrepancy as exists at present between the expenditure and the revenue of Canada. I do not suppose it is necessary for me to emphasize that' this so-called war tax is not a war tax, or that not one dollar of it is going to be spent in conducting the war. I have the " Hansard " report of the Minister's Budget speech here, in which he says half a dozen times that every dollar that is to be spent on the war will be borrowed. I. have no fault to find with that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How will the interest be met upon the $150,000,000 that will have been borrowed since the outbreak of war until the end of the fiscal year 1915-16? It amounts to about $7,000,000, and is in consolidated revenue expenditure. I should like to point out that according to my estimate the special taxes will raise an amount slightly in excess of that which will be required to pay the interest upon the amount that will he borrowed for our war expenditure.

That is exactly what I
have been trying to make clear to my hon. friend all along. I am saying that this money that my hon. friend is proposing to raise by taxes and by the increased tariff is for the ordinary consolidated expenditure, and that interest on the public debt is part of the consolidated expenditure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And for war.

Interest on our public
debt will be paid out of consolidated revenue. But granted that my hon. friend is correct in the suggestion he makes that it would take about $7,000,000, let me point out that he is asking for from between

$8,000,000 and $10,000,000 direct taxes and between $22,000,000 and $25,000,000 indirect taxes. That is not all for interest, even taking my hon. friend's own statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How is the pension list to be taken care of?
Has my hon. friend paid any pension list?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, but I am afraid we will have to.
What I object to is that my hon. friend tries to make the people believe that these taxes are for the war, whereas they are not for the war at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are.

I did not want to take
the time of the House to read my hon. friend's remarks, but I am afraid that I shall be obliged to. He is reported to have said-
What about the wai tax legislation of the United States? There is no war at all.

I am delighted that the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Mac-donell) has asked me that question, Because it is a matter I had in my mind and I perhaps would have forgotten it if he had not mentioned it. My hon. friend brought that matter up last night. Did the United States put on an extra duty to raise that tax?
They did.
What on?

They put it on a
very great number of articles. The list is quite as comprehensive as the list in the resolution before this House, and it contains additional matters, but the items that are taxed in our resolution are almost all included in the American Bill.
Not tariff taxation at all.
Yes.

No, my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonell) is mistaken in that. The United States, on account of the falling revenue, put direct taxes largely on the line of the direct taxes suggested by the Minister of Finance.
And a stamp tax, too.
A stamp tax, certainly, but they did not raise the tariff.

I did not say that
they did raise the tariff.
Yes.

No, I never said so
and do not intend to say so to-night.

That is just exactly what I wanted to tell my hon. friend that the United States put on direct taxes, a stamp tax, a tax on railway and steamship tickets, just along the line followed by the Minister of Finance, but every dollar that the United States levies goes direct into the treasury, whereas, as a result of what my hon. friend is doing in making a horizontal increase in the tariff, $1 goes into the treasury and from $4 to $5 into the pockets of the manufacturers. That suits the hon. member for South Toronto. He represents a constituency where they are all manufacturers and where there are no farmers. I do not object to him being pleased; I think he has got his way. The manufacturers have made this tariff or they might have made it. They could not have made it any better for themselves. I doubt if they made it, because if they had made it they never would have raised it as high.
They would not have had the nerve.

The manufacturers have considerable nerve, but I do not think that they would have had that much nerve. If my hon. friend had followed the example of the United States he would not have proposed to lhave increased the tariff at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But they are not at war.

No, but there was a depression just the same as there is here, and it was before the war just as it was here before the war. My hon. friends opposite at least do not need to take the word of any hon. gentleman on this side of the House. Let them read the statement of Sir Edmund Osier, president of the Dominion Bank, and the statement of the general manager of the Bank of Nova Scotia, and see what they say. They say that the war might in some degree have aggravated it, but that the depression was 'here, that it had been coming, that they had foreseen it, that they had warned the people about it, and that it was not caused by the war. As far as we are concerned, speaking for the province I come from, and I know it applies to Manitoba and Alberta in the same way, from the money point of

view, the war is a godsend. Nothing finer from a financial point of view ever happened the West.
That is what Sir Edmund Osier says, too.
Is that the member for Toronto?

Yes, that is the same Sir Edmund Osier. Nothing better ever happened us. We had thousands and thousands of unemployed men in our cities there that we did not know what to do with. They have gone to the war, and they are earning good wages. If we want to sell wheat, oats, barley, horses, cattle, sheep or hogs we can sell them at good prices. Except. in that portion of the country where they had no crop at all, where they suffered from drouth, the farmers were better off last year than the year before. .This Government cannot put the blame of the hard times on the war. The war has been a godsend to them in many ways. This raising of the tariff that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance is proposing is just simply carrying out the promise made by gentlemen on that side of the House to the manufacturers prior to the election of 1911 for the support and subscriptions that they then received. They are carrying out and fulfilling a promise that up to the present tune they did not dare to carry out, they did not dare to fulfil, and if it had not been for the war they would not have dared to fulfil it now. If there were no war, and if the Finance Minister came down with such a precious proposition as that which he has before the House today, why, they would be wiped out of existence. The Minister, notwithstanding the unfortunate position of Canada, has brought forward this measure to add burdens to the backs of the people in order to fulfil a promise made to the manufacturers in 1911.
_ I have been dealing with this question in a general way; now, I want to deal in a more concrete manner with one or two items. The hon. member for South Toronto said last night in his speech:
The proposed taxation does not fall on the farmer or on the working man, and both these classes are thoroughly satisfied with thexBudget as it stands at present. They ought to be satisfied.
Just read the next paragraph.

Cannot all axle grease
be made in Canada?

It is possible that in
my hon. friend's part of the country they may make their butter poor enough so that it can be put into axle grease, and therefore it can be made in Canada.
What about the real question: cannot the axle grease be made in Canada? Axle grease is largely used in nearly every part of the country, and is it not nearly all made in Canada now?

If my hon. friend is
correct in that, - why does the Minister of Finance put an extra 5 per cent duty on for the benefit of the manufacturer. If all the axle grease is made in Canada now, is the increased duty going to give him any more revenue? But the farmer pays it all the same.
The following table which I have prepared will show the former British preference duty on articles largely used; the percentage of increase in the British preference under the proposal now made by the Finance Minister, as well as the former general tariff duty on these articles and the percentage of increase now proposed, and in every item it will be seen that the British preference gets the worst of it.

Their salaries are
better.
fMr. Turriff.]

This table shows what
my hon. friend the Minister of Finance is doing to encourage trade with Great Britain. We had an example this afternoon from my hon. friend the member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham). He told us what hon. gentlemen on the other side think of the preference to Great Britain. He had no use for it. My hon. friend the member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) made the same statement a few years ago. " Give us," he said, " a majority in the House, and we will show you what we will do with the British prefer-

ence." My hon. friends opposite now have a majority and they have shown us what they propose to do with the British preference. This Government could have got along perfectly well without increasing the tariff; but not satisfied with increasing the general tariff, they have undertaken to increase the tariff on the goods that we are bringing in from Great Britain. My hon. friend the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) stated yesterday that there was a great deal of difficulty in bring-
10 p.m. ing in goods from Great Britain, owing to the extra freight and shortage of boats.
My hon. friends opposite now propose an extra tax on British goods for the purpose of shutting off trade with Great Britain. The tax is put on for no other reason. If my hon. friend the Minister of Finance has to have more money, if the Government will not shut off expenditure, if it is bound to have an extra $30,000,000, impose the taxes on the outside world; and if you cannot do it in that way, impose a direct tax and take your $10,000,000; tax the banks and the trust companies and the insurance companies; tax every one, make them pay what money you want; but for Heaven's sake keep your unholy and disloyal hands off the British preference.
Three or four years ago we were told throughout the West that because we advocated a free market in the United States in which to sell our goods, we were hardly loyal.
Disloyal.

That we were absolutely disloyal, as my hon. friend has remarked. Let us see what the position is now. I do not want to draw invidious comparisons between one part of the country and the *other; but many people down East called us disloyal because we wanted to sell our crops in the best market. I think I am justified in pointing out what has taken place in the last six months. Have our friends in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, the three provinces that were picked out as holding many disloyal people because they wanted to sell their crops in [DOT]the best markets-have they shown themselves less loyal than others? Have they been less ready to volunteer for service on The firing line than people in any other part of Canada?
Many of those who voted against reciprocity have gone to the front.

I do not doubt that. I have said, time and again, in this House
that I have never met a disloyal Conservative nor a disloyal Liberal, so far as I know, in my life. I should be sorry to think that there were many disloyal people in Canada. There are many kinds of loyalty. One kind consists in supplying good goods for the use of the army.
Let me point out another thing that has taken place in the West. The Grain Growers' Association of Manitoba, the Grain Growers' Association of Saskatchewan, the United Farmers of Alberta have all, at their conventions, held during the past few months, carried unanimously resolutions calling on this Government to do away with the duties against Great Britain and to make up any lack of revenue that may follow by a direct tax on the land-on the farmers' land. And, remember, there is no politics in these organizations; they are composed of Liberals and Conservatives alike. And these are the people who a few years ago were accused of disloyalty by the very men who, now that Great Britain is in trouble, now that she is fighting the fight of her life, fighting for her national existence and ours, and when her success depends upon her commerce, come forward and say: We will help you by sending some, men, but with the other hand we wiV try to cut your throat by preventing your | oods from coming into Canada. And I say again, once let the people of Canada realize the position-
Louder.

Oh, I will speak loud enough for the people in the West to hear; don't you fear. I say, let the peop'e of Canada realize the position, and mj hon. friend the Solicitor General will be piping lower instead of louder than he is now.
I have another list here, a long one also, in which the increases against Great Britain and against the United States are exactly the same. I have another list in which the percentage of increase is somewhat larger against the United States and the rest of the world than it is against Great Britain. I have selected these items from the tariff because they particularly affect the settlers of the West.
There has been a good deal of talk in the last month or two about greater production. Our friends the manufacturers sent a delegation to Winnipeg to meet with the grain growers. They proposed that an extra million acres of wheat should be sown next spring-that new lands should be broken to the extent of a million acres and wheat sown. No farmer would ever have suggested

that. Any one who knows anything about farming in the West knows that you might just as well throw your seed away as sow it on the sod. You would not get a crop worth harvesting. The farmers showed that this was not practicable. Then it was proposed that $50,000,000 should be borrowed by this Government to place people on the land. The cry was " Back to t'he land." Mr. Speaker, it is not necessary to borrow $50,000,000 to get people to go on the land. Nor is it necessary to tell the farmers to put in a million acres extra of wheat. The farmer is not a fool altogether. He will put in an extra crop if that crop is going to pay him. All you have to do to get the farmer to put in all the land possible, all you have to do in order to get the people back to the land, is to make, the conditions such that they can make a good living out of the land. But what is the Government doing? It is putting a load on the back of the farmer. The Grain Growers' Guide put it very well a month or so ago when it said: Just let the manufacturers get off the farmer's back and there will be no trouble about oack to the land and no trouble about production.
Just one word further about the effect of these extra taxes on the farmers. As soon as this war is over and the price of wheat goes down to normal again, and while this added burden remains, hundreds and thousands on the western plains will leave the land. Why? Because they cannot make a living on the land under the circumstances. The Minister of hnanee is putting on these extra duties. But will he take off these duties and put the tariff back where it was as soon as the war is over? He will do nothing of the kind. Those taxes are there to stay, as long as the hon. gentlemen opposite can keep them there. When the war is over the argument will be: We have created vested interests; you cannot now take off this protection, for it would mean failure among the manufacturers. So these burdens are added to the burdens of the farmers and artisans; living is made more expensive; conditions will be worse for workingman and farmer. And what are the compensating advantages? Practically there are none.
My hon. friend from West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham)-and I do not intend to follow him back for five thousand years and all over the face of the earth-said that unemployment was an issue at the present time. Yes, and it was an issue prior to 1896. But it was not an issue from 1896 to 1911. But hon. gentlemen opposite are back

in power, and unemployment is once more an issue. The hon. gentleman stated also that two days' work a week, at eight hours a day, should be sufficient, if everybody worked, to produce all that is being produced at this time. I do not blame my hon. friend for trying to bring the labour. ing classes to that point of view, because under this Government and under the tariff they have enacted, two days' work a week is about all that the working people are going to be able to get in the near future. So my hon. friend, I think, is quite right in bringing that forward. My hon. friend also stated that Great Britain had not been able to get one follower in the line of free trade; but he forgot to mention that to-day free trade Great Britain is financing the world. Where are all the protective nations getting their money to carry on the war? From Great Britain. Were it not for being able to get money in Great Britain we could not take part in the war, because the minister has to borrow every dollar to send our forces there-and $30,000,000 more. My hon. friend said that when British preference was introduced it came very near putting the pottery works at St. Johns right out of business. The preferential duty against Great Britain on pottery ware was 20 per cent. Now it is going to he 25 per cent. I say if the potteries in St. Johns, with a protection of 20 per cent . and with high rates of transportation on that class of goods, cannot live, in the name of common sense let them shut up business and go into something that can get on with 20 per cent protection and allow some revenue to come into the treasury of Canada. The business that cannot live under these circumstances is not worth preserving in Canada. It is out of place in Canada, where there are many factories that we are bolstering up with new protection, the money invested in which would be far better invested in something that would pay a reasonable return-and there are in Cafiada many opportunities for the investing of money.

My hon. friend has not answered the question as to his opinion of the argument of my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) that the tax on bituminous coal should not go on because it will be too hard on the railways that consume the coal.

I agree that the tax on
bituminous coal should not go on. I do not believe that one of the taxes imposed should go on. An additional objection is that it will put an argument into the hands of the
/

railway companies for an increase in freight rates when they have to pay 10 cents a ton more for coal. Is my hon. friend satisfied to put on an extra 10 cents on coal for the railroads and have every one of the farmers he represents pay extra freight rates to make up the additional cost of coal to the railway companies?

I have not said so. We are taxing the consumers of coal, but the hon. member for Halifax objects to that because the railways have to pay and argues that they cannot stand it. I am asking the opinion of my hon. friend who now has the Floor upon this point.
If you are asking for the opinion of the hon. member for Halifax, he is able to express his own opinions.
Your opinion.

I am against the extra
taxes on coal and on everything else the minister is taxing. I would say not to put on any of the taxes, and then you would suit me and my hon. friend to the right (Mr. A. K. Maclean).
My hon. friend from South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) yesterday said that it was necessary for the Government to pay those cash subsidies to Mackenzie and Mann in order that the bonds guaranteed by this Government and by many of the provincial governments might not become a charge on the respective Governments that guaranteed them. If the Government are running away with the idea that by giving the cash subsidy they have given to the Canadian Northern railway they are going to relieve this Government or any other Provincial Government from the guarantees of bonds that they have made, they are making a great mistake. They are only putting off the evil day for a few years, and the day will come before very long when this Government, after having done what they did a year ago, will have to take over the Canadian Northern railway and will have to expend another $50,000,000 in making it fit to compete, and they will add another $300,000,000 to the debt of Canada. They are not obviating any of those results, they are simply putting off the evil day for a very few years.
I only trust that the l\finister of Finance may think better of some of these proposals that he has made and that he will give a little consideration to the view of the farmer and of, the poor man; that he will, if he has to raise money, so arrange his taxes that they will fall not evenly per capita of the
population, but evenly according to the ability of the men to pay. My hon. friend does not care to take up the matter of taxing incomes, or land; but I see by the press that the local government in his own province of Ontario to-day has come forward with a proposition to put a direct tax on all lands in the different municipalities, to raise $1,800,000. Could not the Minister of Finance adopt something on that line? Such a tax would have this advantage, that the man who has property worth $1,000 would only pay one-tenth as much as the man with $10,000 worth, whereas all I can say in favour of the proposition of the Minister of Finance is that he is following out one of the biblical rules that to him that hath shall be given and from him that hath not shall be taken even that which he hath.
Mr. WM. WRIGHT (Muskoka):	There
are many matters that come before this House which receive a measure of consideration, are dealt with by Parliament, are recorded in the statute-book, or pass into oblivion, and we hear no more of them in this House. But that hardy annual, the Budget speech, buds and blossoms and sheds its fragrance over this House once a year, and gentlemen on the Government side seem to be quite satisfied with the perfume; but gentlemen on the opposite side, for some reason, seem to become irritated. It is very peculiar how we differ with regard to these matters.
The Budget brings before us many matters for our consideration, among others the trade policy. How shall we raise the revenue? The people have come to be divided into three schools. We have those who believe that free trade should be the dominant consideration in any tariff. Then there are those who believe that protection should be kept to the front, and there are those who believe that we should attach more importance to a tariff for revenue. The Budget now before us is known- as the war Budget, and as far as I have been able to put my finger upon the pulse of public opinion I have found that the general opinion of this country favours the proposals of the Finance Minister. So far as I have been able to learn very little objection has been raised in the country. It is generally conceded that the tax has been laid upon the public in such a manner as to fall upon those best able to bear it. It is true the non. gentleman who has just taken his seat, and who usually sheds a lot of briny tears over the farmers of the West, objects strenuously, as he always has done

since I have had the pleasure of hearing his voice in this House. I hope the farmers of the West have better friends in this House than the hon. gentleman, for it is well within my recollection that when a move was made by some of us on this side of the House, then in Opposition, to lower the duties on farm implements, a boon we will suppose to the farmers of the West, we met with objections from the hon. gentleman and others associated with him, who were quite satisfied with the tariff as it was;. and as long as his friends were in power, he did not care how high the tariff was against the farmers of the West. I am just reminded by an hon. member that he even spoke against the proposal to lower the duties.
It must be conceded that there is room for honest difference of opinion with regard to the exigencies of tariff. Under the proposals before the House the duties generally are being raised 7J per cent, and the duties against Great Britain only 5 per cent. It is true that the hon. gentleman who preceded me, by figuring out on percentages, tried to show that the people of Great Britain were not favoured under the present proposals to the same extent as the manufacturers of the United States. I want to unqualifiedly deny that. The people of Great Britain have the advantage of a 5 per cent increase against a per cent increase against the United States and other countries. An effort is being made, and no doubt will be made, if we are to judge by what has been said by hon. gentlemen opposite and the press who support them, to fasten a charge of disloyalty upon the Conservative party for having slightly increased the duty on goods coming from Great Britain. I do not believe that any charge of disloyalty can. he laid against the Conservative party on that score. The people of Great Britain have a tariff that we will suppose suits themselves; they adjust it with a view to the needs of Great Britain, and the colonies have no preference whatever, not a particle, in the tariff arrangements of Great Britain. In fact when we look into the figures we find exactly the .opposite. While a great country like Germany is able to send practically all she produces into Great Britain duty free, some .of the colonies are taxed and taxed very heavily on their goods going into Great Britain. One would naturally think from listening to the discussion on free trade that Great Britain allows all goods to enter free of customs duty, but such is far indeed from being the case. Let me read some of the duties that are collected at the

ports of Great Britain annually on various articles:

These figures do not include what is collected by the Isle of Man, the figures for which were $466,690. I would point out that that sum is vastly in excess of the whole customs duties of the Dominion of Canada. By way of illustration, I will just refer to the item of tea. As I pointed out a moment ago, Germany has free access to Britain on practically every thing she produces, while a country that lives under the British flag and whose people recognize the King of England as their King is taxed $25,000,000 out of the $30,000,000 collected by Great Britain on tea. I am only pointing that out to show that the colonies get no favours from Great Britain with regard to tariff. In fact, it is just the opposite, but I am not charging Great Britain with disloyalty on that account. She makes her tariff to suit herself, and while the peculiar brand of free trade that prevails there may suit the British people, I do not believe that it would as well suit the people of Canada.

I have listened with
much interest to the list which my hon. friend has just read. Let me ask him whether a single product of Canada pays a dollar of duty when it enters Great Britain?

I should not like to say, because I am not familiar with everything that is produced in Canada. I should imagine we produce some sugar and other articles in this country, but I do not know whether they are exported to Great Britain. What I was saying was that some of the articles in this list are produced in British colonies.

I am speaking of
Canada.

Let me point out that while this may suit the people of Great Britain-it is absolutely unsuited to the

people of Canada. Taking up for a moment that item of tea, I want to show how the duty is levied and the unfairness of it. Let us take some poor person in Great Britain, some washerwoman, or some people in poor circumstances, who wish to go and have their tea. They buy tea worth 20 cents a pound, but they pay five pence, or ten cents, a pound duty; so that the washerwoman pays a 100 per cent duty on her tea. The rich chocolate manufacturer, who is protected up to the hilt, the iron manufacturer, the lord of the manor, or the wealthy gentleman who uses tea that costs $4 or $5 a pound pays ten cents a pound duty; in other words, he pays ten per cent duty while the very poor pay a 100 per cent duty. That may be good enough for the people of Great Britain, but it is not good enough for the people of this country. I have no objection to this tariff so long as it is confined within the borders of Great Britain.
Are we in a position to follow the example of Great Britain in regard to trade matters? When Great Britain adopted the present policy she was then the greatest manufacturing- nation on earth; she had become so under a very strong protective tariff which had been kept upon the statute books for centuries. After they had become the greatest manufacturing nation upon earth, after they had found that they could not raise enough food to feed themselves, and after they found that they had to import immense quantities of raw material, they said: We are the greatest trading nation on earth; we have to buy and sell abroad and we believe that free trade would work out to our advantage. Are we in that position to-day? Have we ever been in that position? Have we ever been in such a position that we can call ourselves the greatest manufacturing nation on earth? Have we ever been in a position where we had to import nearly all of the food we consumed, or have we ever been in a position where we had to import all our raw materials from across the sea? We have never been in that position and I look over the pages of history and look in vain to see the name of a single country that ever started and became the biggest and foremost manufacturing nation and did it under free trade. It is true that Great Britain has a very great trade to-day, much greater than it had when she took up the policy of free trade. It is, true that the trade of Canada is much greater than when we first adopted the policy of protection, it is true that the United States have a much greater trade 28
than they had when they first adopted protection, and it is true that Germany and France are greater to-day than ever they were before. The thing is true of all the prominent nations of the earth; so that the fact that Great Britain's trade is greater tnan it was proves absolutely nothing in favour of free trade.
I think it is manifest to every man that the nation beginning at the bottom which wishes to build up its industries must from the very nature of things give a certain measure of protection to its industries for a time at least, and that is just what we are doing in Canada. That has been the policy followed by the Conservative party and that has been the policy followed by the Reform party. The only difference between us is that we practise what we preach and hon. gentlemen opposite preach one thing and when they get on the treasury benches they practise the very opposite. I fancy the people of this country have come to look upon the gentlemen, who now occupy the benches opposite as being absolutely unreliable in regard to any trade policy. They cannot fail to remember the claims that were made during the years they were in opposition, they cannot fail to remember how the manufacturers were described as robbers and thieves, they lacked adjectives to adequately describe the people who happened to be engaged in manufacturing. We can remember that old knight of blue ruin who used to go up and down the concessions and side roads and picture to the farmers the awful conditions under which they lived. These hon. gentlemen said: Just let us into power and we will do away with every vestige of protection. The right hon. gentleman who now leads the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), on the platform in Winnipeg, when looking out on those vast prairies of the West, said: Put us in power and we will give you free trade as they have it in Britain. At that very time, Mr. Speaker, they had a hard-and-fast bargain with the big manufacturers that they should keep the protection that they had if they only helped them to get into power. On the strength of that bargain these big manufacturers stood behind them and helped them into power, and they got the advantage when these hon. gentlemen got into office. They put the duties into such shape as to help the large manufacturers. When it was pointed out that in raising these duties they were hurting the farmers of the country, they said: So much the worse for the farmers; the manufacturers are something tangible, we



can keep hold of them and we propose to keep them. Then they made an effort to hoodoo the farmers into the belief that they were doing something for them. The present Government has done more to reduce the duties in two or three years than was done by these hon. gentlemen during the fifteen years that they were in power.
A great deal has been said as to the assistance that was given to Great Britain by what is termed the British preference. I am willing to concede everything to hon. gentlemen opposite that they are entitled to, and to admit that they did put a British preference upon the statute books, which before the introduction of the present Budget amounted to 33J per cent. Let us give hon. gentlemen opposite credit for whatever they did in that regard. But, before they adopted the preference, they raised the duties on a large number of articles we import from Britain, and they lowered the duties upon, or made free, a large number of articles coming from the	United	States, so thatwhen the preference went into effect people in Great Britain who wanted to get into our markets were in as bad a position as before the preference went on. Looking it over and figuring it out, Mr. Speaker, you will find that for every $100 worth of goods that came in from Great Britain, $25 worth came in free under the Tariff Act. You will find that under that beautiful arrangement 45 per cent of goods from the United States were brought into this country free. This is what these hon. gentlemen were doing for England. In the two or three years since the present Government came into power, the percentage has remained about the same, namely, about 25 per cent coming in free from Great Britain; but there are only 37 per cent of goods coming in free from the United States. Britain has received an advantage equivalent to 8 per cent in her favour since the present Government came	into	power	in	respect to	thefree	list. That	is something	wehave done for the people of Great Britain or for the people of this country, because I have always been at a loss to follow the reasoning of our free trade friends. They tell us that the consumer always pays the duty, and yet they said they were doing a great	deal for Great
Britain, they lowered the duty to some extent on goods coming from there. How the preference could be of any particular advantage to Great Britain, if the people of Canada got the whole benefit of it, is one of these things that it is very difficult to understand, but hon. gentlemen

opposite are always arguing on both sides of the question.
I will follow the hon. member (Mr. Turriff) for a few minutes in some of the claims he has put forward. He told us that he would lower the expenditure so that it would equal the revenue, but what he means by that I do not quite understand. The present Government takes the ground that it would not be in the interests of the people of Canada to cut down the expenditure to a very large extent suddenly. They have cut down all the controllable expenditure that they could, and they have taken what I consider fair and just means to increase the revenue. I think we can safely leave it to the people of Canada as to whether the proposition advanced by the hon. member or the policy of the Government is the wiser. The hon. gentleman told us that the Government had been paying huge sums to Mackenzie and Mann and to the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, but I would remind him that the present Government is not responsible for either of these great enterprises, both of which were carried forward to such an advanced stage by the late Government that it would have been against the interests of the country to stop them now. The hon. gentlemen opposite are responsible for the initiation of these two transcontinental enterprises which were designed to be completed about the same time. When they are completed there will be two transcontinental roads in competition with the Canadian Pacific railway, or three transcontinental roads competing for the business that had up to the present time been done by one road. I think, Mr. Speaker, that the Liberal Government ought not to have given the assistance they gave to either one of these roads, or that they should have forced the two to amalgamate, and thus give us one great trunk transcontinental line in competition with the Canadian Pacific railway, which, I think, would be sufficient. I believe an arrangement could have been entered into, between the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Northern railway, by which one of these lines would have answered every purpose. At all events the present Government is not responsible for the undertaking of these two railroads. The hon. gentleman told us that a large number of buildings had been erected during the last year in little villages and town all over Canada, but my information is that there were only two or three public buildings erected during the whole course of last summer in comparatively small places, and none of these were erected in places of 300

population as the hon. gentleman said. If there is such a ease it certainly has never come to my knowledge and it does not exist, as the hon. gentleman said it did, in the province of Ontario. As the hour is late, Mr. Speaker, I beg to move the adjournment of the debate.
